News.title: How fake pregnancy spiralled into horror newborn kidnap plot after desperate mum-to-be suffers 3 traumatic miscarriages
News.content:
ON THEIR wedding day, they danced joyously to “their special song”, Unchained Melody, as family and friends cheered them on.

Nine years later, Eleonor Alejandra Mendoza and her husband Arturo, unexpectedly heard it played again, but his time while they were in the back of a police car after having been arrested for the kidnapping of a baby.



The extraordinary story of how a young Mexican woman felt such pressure to give birth in a country where family is everything, that she concocted an elaborate plan to fake her pregnancy, is told in the Netflix documentary A Child of My Own.

What starts as an elaborate lie turned into a complex charade that threatened to upend her life and relationship, and ultimately unleashed a media scandal that shook the country.



“I was drawn into problems that got bigger and bigger,” says Ale.

“And I started making decisions and taking actions which got more complicated, until there was no way out. No turning back.”



The documentary is told in an imaginative way by Oscar-nominated director, Maite Alberdi, in which the first half plays out like a drama with actors in the roles of the principal characters in an extended flashback, while the second half features interviews with Alejandra and Arturo, explaining their actions first-hand.

The pair married in July 2000 when Eleonor, known as Ale, was just 17.



“I was pregnant and that’s part of the reason we got married then but I also loved Arturo,” she says.

“I always dreamed of being a mum and I was full of hope.

“I have a large family. All my cousins are mums. I felt like it was fulfilling my dream by having a family of my own.

“When I got married, I felt pressured to please Arturo’s family. I didn’t feel accepted by his mum and that made me want to do everything I could to win her over.”

Ale was devasted when she miscarried while living with her in-laws and felt the “blame” lying heavily on her shoulders.



“I was crying in my bedroom, not wanting to see anyone but they came up to my room.

“One of Arturo’s aunts said, ‘Why are you crying? We all go through this.’ Then his mum said, ‘You should have been more careful. You can’t behave like that.’”

While family continued to talk about them having kids soon, Ale felt the pressure increasing.



“Soon after that first miscarriage, I was pregnant again.

“Arturo would tell me, ‘You have to be careful. Don’t do this, don’t do that.’

“Then I had a second miscarriage. After a few years we started to worry when I didn’t get pregnant.”

Following fertility treatment, she fell pregnant again in 2009, but while working at The General Hospital in Mexico City as an administrative assistant, she had another miscarriage.

It was then, she says, that she met a young woman called Mayra Navarro Vega who was there because she wanted to have an abortion.



“Mayra told me she already had a baby girl from a different father and that her mum would kick her out of the home if she had another.

“She also said the father wasn’t accepting any responsibility, because he didn’t believe the baby wasn’t his.

“Then she said, ‘I’d rather give it away than throw it away.’ I asked her if she was serious, and she said, ‘Yes.’”

The pair then agreed an audacious deal to secretly give the baby to Ale.

“When I got home, I decided I wouldn’t tell anyone that I had lost the baby, especially not Arturo. I didn’t want anyone saying it was my fault, again.”



Instead, she began eating lots of calorific food to put on “pregnancy weight” month by month, going from 119 pounds to 143, 176, all the way to 216.

“My tummy really looked like I was pregnant and I felt so special because people close to you start treating you so lovingly and come up and touch your belly so sweetly.”

Mayra told her that the due date was the week of 16 June, and that the doctors thought it was a girl.

While working in the hospital, Ale looked at the ultrasound Mayra had of her baby and brought a picture of it home to show the family.

Arturo was happy, even though he wanted a baby boy.



When his mum told Ale that she didn’t look like she was carrying a girl, Ale replied that doctors should know better than old wives’ tales of being able to tell the sex from the shape of a woman’s belly.

On a shopping trip with Arturo to buy maternity clothes, she mentioned a baby that her friend was adopting and became upset when Arturo said that he could never adopt because it’s not the same as flesh and blood.

Ale tried to put on a happy face at a baby shower for family and friends but she was feeling the strain of her lie.

“It was awful, seeing everybody happy, my parents, my family, my grandma. I wanted someone to burst that balloon of lies. To spill everything out.”

It was when she was unable to stop Arturo from accompanying her to a doctor for a medical in order to get her maternity leave, that she thought the truth would be revealed.



As Arturo sat in the room, she told the doctor that she was 38 weeks gone.

Then came the moment she was dreading, as he listened to the baby’s heartbeat but couldn’t hear one.

Thinking it was the fault of the device he was using, the doctor went and got an old-fashioned type, and this time, to her disbelief, he said he could hear the baby.

“The doctor gave me my 90 days of maternity leave. I was thinking, ‘Am I pregnant? I lost it, didn’t I? Did I get pregnant again?’ Too much was messed up in my head.”

When Mayra gave birth, Ale pretended to the hospital that she was her neighbour and wanted to see her.



In the ward, Mayra had a fever but pointed to the baby and said the deal was still in place.

“I was holding the baby, when around two or three in the afternoon, a man arrived. He turned out to the be the baby’s father and he took the baby from me and held her.”

Ale walked out and returned later, after visiting hours ended, and says that Mayra was getting dressed to leave.

“I said, ‘You can’t leave me here with her. We have to do this right,’ but Mayra replied, “I did my part. Take the baby.”

Ale put the tiny four and a half pounds tot in a shopping bag and walked out of the hospital. This was later found to have been captured on CCTV camera, which is shown in the documentary.



Outside, she was startled by her husband arriving, who asked her what she was doing. Ale got in the car, with the baby still in the bag, and confessed to what she had done.

Stunned, he angrily ordered her out of the car, telling her to give the baby back.

But he eventually relented and she got back in and they booked into a hotel for the night to talk things over.

Here, Arturo asked her what the plan was going to be. She explained, “Mayra was going to be discharged tomorrow morning. I was going to pretend to be her relative to expediate things.

“By the time you got to the hospital, I’d have the baby, and the paperwork.”



Still angry and shouting, he eventually calmed down enough to hold the baby, telling her, “You’ll be happy with us.”

The three of them fell asleep on the bed, until they were awoken by the police pounding on the door.

They took the baby away and arrested the pair for kidnap, while Ale screamed that the baby had been given to her.

“We were in the police car when on the radio they started playing Unchained Melody, the song we danced to at our wedding,” she recalls.

“It was our special song and, at that moment, I thought, it was a sign. We love each other. We’ll be okay.”



That was Ale’s story and she has stuck by it ever since.

However, Mayra and the baby’s father firmly dispute this and say that their baby, Katya, was simply kidnapped.

A court found Ale guilty of kidnapping and she was given a 13-year prison sentence.

Arturo was locked up for two and a half years until the end of the trial when he was acquitted.

“At the time I felt that Ale had done something unforgivable and that she was evil and I didn’t want to see her again,” says Arturo.



“But being in jail gives you a lot of time to think things over. I reflected on where I might have failed as a partner.

“When I said, ‘I don’t want to adopt, I want a child of my flesh and blood,’ maybe I contributed to closing myself off in that way.

“I admit I did push her a bit, because I wanted to be a dad and I wanted to have a son.”

Once released, he started writing to his wife in prison saying that he forgave her and that he loved her with all his heart.

In the documentary, Mayra gives her side of the story.



“There was never a deal,” she says.

“I didn’t meet her until Katya was born. I only went to the hospital to give birth.

“I had my pregnancy check-ups in another health facility, so I never got to see Ale any earlier.”

Documents confirmed this.

Mayra had not been at the hospital until a few weeks before she gave birth.



“When I was in the hospital, Ale wandered over and showed me her hospital ID badge and said she was doing a survey and she asked me questions like, Was this my first baby? Was she from the same marriage? How was my relationship with her dad?

“That’s where she got all the information.”

Ale denies this but a folder with surveys inside was found beside her jumper and ID badge at the hospital.

There is also footage taken by Katya’s father on his phone, of him tenderly holding his new-born daughter in hospital and talking sweetly to her.

“I had a fever of almost 104F,” says Mayra.



“I couldn’t be discharged because I had an infection. I was asked for urine samples so I left the room and when I returned, my baby was gone.

“My first thought was that maybe a nurse had taken her for a bath or to feed her.

“I never thought she had been stolen.”

The documentary shows Ale being released from prison, having served her sentence, and being reunited with Arturo, who tells her, “It’s over, my love.”

But in a further twist, his yearning to have a son, caused them to part – temporarily.



“Soon after leaving prison, Arturo told me he still wanted to be a dad,” explains Ale.

“I replied that he had the right to pursue his happiness but that I wasn’t willing to undergo any treatment, and with me, he wasn’t going to be a dad.

“We were separated for a while, we gave each other space, and he had a short relationship with another woman and a son was born.

“After that, Arturo came back looking for me.

“We talked and he told me what had happened.



“He said that he missed me, that he loved me, and that he wanted me in his life.

“He asked me to try again and I decided to do so.

“It makes me happy to see him fulfilled as a father.

“But even more, it makes me happy that he sees me in his life as the other parent figure of his child.”

News.title: Dangerous criminals including sex offenders are released daily, top cop warns – after blunders left killer free to roam
News.content:
DANGEROUS criminals including vile sex offenders are being released on bail every day, Britain’s top cop has warned.

Metropolitan Police chief Sir Mark Rowley admitted his force “could have done better” after serial killer Simon Levy was allowed to roam the streets.



Levy, 40, unleashed a sadistic rampage across London last year during which he murdered two women and raped a third while on bail.

He was jailed for life yesterday after killing Carmenza Valencia Trujillo, 53, and Sheryl Wilkins, 39, amid a string of missed chances to stop him.



Two officers, a police constable and a detective sergeant at the Met are now being probed by the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC).

While accepting his force’s failings in the case, Rowley slammed the justice system for putting dangerous lags “back on the streets”.

He vowed the Met would do “everything we can do”, but accused the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) of ignoring police warnings over Levy.

Rowley told BBC’s Today programme: “He was repeatedly, by the police, put before the courts seeking remanding in custody.



“The police were saying this guy is too dangerous to be on the streets, and between [the CPS] and the courts, they kept bailing him.

“We’re seeing far too many cases day in and day out – knife carriers, sex offenders – who are being bailed.

“A few years ago, they would have been remanded in custody, and we can’t carry all of that load in communities.

“We will do everything we can do to do better – but the justice system needs to carry more of the load than it is at the moment rather than passing it back onto the streets.”

Rowley described the situation as a “whole system failing”, after Levy was previously jailed for groping two women at music festivals in 2018.



He was caged for three years in September 2021 over the attacks, but was released from prison in February 2023.

Levy was subject to a sexual offenders’ order and should have been carefully monitored – but was instead left free to kill and assault.

The killer remained free to strike repeatedly, despite continually coming to the attention of the law.



Following his release from jail, Levy was arrested on suspicion of murder and twice charged with groping women on the Tube, but freed each time.

He also failed to appear at three crown court hearings over the sexual assaults on trains – but no warrant was ever sought for his arrest.

Levy killed Carmenza, before dumping her body in the stairwell of a derelict building in Peckham, South East London, on March 17 last year.

Five months later, he murdered Sheryl near a B&M store in Tottenham, North London.

The Met had previously closed the investigation from the January rape, despite the victim knowing where Levy lived.



And officers did not formally interview her until after he had carried out the double murder.

By the time of the second murder, Levy had been arrested three times by the British Transport Police for a string of sex attacks on the Tube.

But the serial sex attacker was granted bail each time.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

He was also arrested over Carmenza’s murder but was released under investigation – leaving him free to kill again.

The Metropolitan Police, British Transport Police and Crown Prosecution Service admitted failings in how they dealt with Levy.

News.title: When will the A31 open? What National Highways has said after New Forest fire closed major road
News.content:
THE A31 has been closed all week after a van fire spread into the nearby New Forest.

Hampshire and Isle of Wight Fire and Rescue Service (HIWFRS) received more than 160 emergency calls reporting a vehicle fire on the eastbound A31 at around 5:24pm on Sunday August 9.



The flames spread to the central reservation before reaching heathland that forms part of the New Forest.

The road has remained since Sunday, causing lengthy diversions and delays for drivers – here’s what we know about when it will reopen.



When will the A31 open?

According to National Highways, the A31 is unlikely to re-open until at least Thursday, August 20, due to ongoing repair works.

A statement from HIWFRS read: “Alongside colleagues from other fire services, we have been using various different techniques to support firefighting efforts, including mulching and tree felling.



“Specialists in a technique known has backburning have been brought in to purposefully burn away strips of heathland, in a controlled way, in order to remove available fuels, creating a fire break which helps to prevent the blaze from spreading further.”

Repair works will only get underway once National Highways have been given clearance from the HIWFRS to access the area.

The statement continued: “Wind is blowing smoke from the fire into the direction of Roger Penny Way, so we ask that you drive with caution in that particular area.

“Our teams continue to make good progress, but we still expect to be on the scene for the next few days, with the A31 remaining closed.”



Due to the road closure, drivers are being advised to allow extra time for their journeys while ensuring they have enough fuel and water.

An area spanning roughly 1.6 kilometres has been affected by the fire, meaning repairs are required on 1,000 metres of boundary fencing.

What is the A31 diversion route?

National Highways has urged drivers not to follow their satnavs and to use the official local diversion instead.

It has also asked motorists to stick to speed limits on local roads and watch out for the New Forest’s livestock, which roams freely.

Westbound motorists should leave the M27 at junction 2 (Ower Interchange) and use the A326 and A35 through Ashurst, Lyndhurst, Allum Green, Hinton Admiral and Christchurch.



At the Iford roundabout they should take the third exit onto the A3060, then the third exit at the Cooper Dean roundabout onto the A338, travelling north to rejoin the A31 at Ashley Heath.

Eastbound drivers should leave the A31 at the Ashley Heath roundabout onto the A338 and continue south towards Bournemouth.

At the Cooper Dean roundabout they should take the first exit onto the A3060, then the first exit at the Iford roundabout onto the A35 through Christchurch, Hinton Admiral, Allum Green, Lyndhurst and Ashurst, before heading north on the A326 to rejoin the M27 at junction 2.

News.title: Tragic details revealed after boy, 7, drowned alongside hero cousin, 15, and her mum on family holiday to seaside
News.content:
BEACH TRAGEDY Tragic details revealed after boy, 7, drowned alongside hero cousin, 15, and her mum on family holiday to seaside

A YOUNG boy who drowned alongside his 15-year-old cousin and her mum on a family holiday suffered a fatal brain injury, an inquest heard.

Musa Ahmed, seven, died in hospital six days after getting into difficulty in the water in West Mersea, Essex, on July 22.



His cousin Sameeha Rahman, 15, and her mother Shelina Rahman, 41, also died in the horror.

An inquest heard today the trio had been on a family holiday at the time of the triple tragedy.



Musa was brought to the shore, stabilised and then flown to the Royal London Hospital, Chelmsford County Hall was told.

Post-mortem examinations gave a provisional cause of death as drowning for all three.



For Musa, hypoxic ischaemic brain injury was also recorded as a provisional cause of death.

Senior coroner for Essex Lincoln Brookes said: “Clearly it is so tragic to come across any death of any individual but when three occur at the same time and of the same family, one cannot underestimate the tragic nature of such an incident.”



Mr Brookes offered his “deepest condolences” to the family, friends and loved ones of the victims.

The coroner adjourned the inquest to January 19, 2027.

Musa, Sameeha and Shelina were among a group of five relatives who were caught up in the horror close to the Sea View Holiday Park.

It is understood the mum and daughter sprang into action in a desperate bid to save Musa from the tide when they got into difficulty themselves.

The dad of the daughter and wife, Dr Mansur Rahman, 49, previously told The Sun he was still suffering from shock and is “fighting to overcome” the tragedy.



He added: “I lost my daughter I lost my wife. Please pray for them.”

In a statement, the boy’s family said: “We would also like to thank the Royal London Hospital intensive care unit team of doctors and nurses who demonstrated outstanding care and dignity for whilst we have been at the hospital.

“We would also like to thank the whole community for their support and prayers.

“We would appreciate privacy during this very difficult time.”

Essex Police have asked anyone who was in the area at the time and has information or footage which could assist their investigation to contact them on 101 and quote incident 1090 of 22 July.

News.title: Terrifying blaze guts FIVE homes as 20 residents evacuated in dead of night and 12 crews battle huge inferno
News.content:
BUNGALOW INFERNO Terrifying blaze guts FIVE homes as 20 residents evacuated in dead of night and 12 crews battle huge inferno

A TERRIFYING blaze has gutted five homes with 20 residents evacuated in the dead of night as fire crews battle the flames.

There were scenes of carnage in Newbridge, South Wales, on Wednesday with the homes left completely devastated.



The inferno ripped through six neighbouring bungalows, completely destroying at least five homes on Hazelwood Road in Pantside.

Shocking images show their charred wreckage as the properties were reduced to burnt-out shells with families’ belongings turned to ash.



Their gardens were also scorched with overhead photos showing a scored landscape from above.

Fire crews descended on the scene yesterday afternoon with locals urged to stay away and keep their windows and doors shut due to smoke.

Around 20 people were supported at temporary accommodation or Newbridge Leisure Centre overnight.

By about 2.30am, all those affected had been checked into a Premier Inn.



The council said it will work with affected families today to arrange longer-term temporary accommodation, while structural engineers assess the damaged properties.

No casualties have been reported and the cause of the fire has yet to be determined.

Fire crews remain at the scene with plumes of smoke still pouring from the wreckage.

Local councillor, Adrian Hussey, told the BBC the houses were absolutely “gutted” with residents’ cars also damaged in the blaze.

He added that residents had attempted to put the fire out themselves but were beaten back by flames.



Julie Nichols, 74, told the broadcaster how she could hear the flames from inside her home and was left in “absolute fear”.

“We were sat in the leisure centre and there were a few people that had actually lost their homes,” she said.

“They were being so brave, I mean to lose everything.”

Newbridge RFC said they were “absolutely heartbroken” in a message on social media and said their clubhouse was open to those affected.

A fundraising page has also been set up by a local resident which said: “There’s a number family’s in Pantside that’s lost everything due to a massive fire that’s spread throughout their homes & gardens.



“As a community I’m praying we can get some sort of fund together to go towards anything they may need. Money isn’t everything but right now any little helps.”

South Wales Fire and Rescue Service said in a statement on Wednesday: “Shortly before 16:00 today, crews were deployed to the scene and a number of resources have been mobilised, including 12 fire appliances, two water bowsers, and an aerial ladder platform.

“Members of the public are urged to stay away from the area to allow emergency services to operate safely and to avoid flying drones, as they can disrupt incident operations.

“Due to smoke in the area, residents are advised to keep windows and doors closed and follow public health advice.”

News.title: Watch droves of ‘selfish’ Brits swarm ‘like ants’ around ITV’s Benidorm hotel pool – forcing family to perch on chairs
News.content:
THIS is the moment a flood of selfish Brits swarmed like ants around ITV’s infamous Benidorm hotel forcing families to perch on chairs.

A mum has now mocked the “selfish middle-aged fellas” she claims queue for hours before charging into the pool area to bag the best sunbeds.



Annie Redfern was staying at Sol Pelicanos Ocas hotel in Benidorm with her partner Declan Nash, 30, and seven-year-old daughter Belle when she witnessed the bizarre poolside battle.

The marketing consultant was stunned to discover holidaymakers had already staked their claim to the loungers before her family had even settled into their ten-night break.



Annie initially arrived at 11.30am to find every sunbed snapped up, but assumed the beds were simply taken because it was midday.

At 6.30am the following day, Annie spotted a huge queue of holidaymakers waiting to bag a lounger – despite the pool not opening until 9am.

She said the crazy daily ritual happened every morning, with the line made up largely of what she described as “middle-aged men”.

As soon as the barrier opened, the sunseekers would swarm like “ants” into the pool area, racing to claim their territory at the hotel, better known as Solana Hotel on the television show

Annie said the sunbed stampede meant her family were forced to perch on plastic chairs if they wanted to spend time beside the pool.

The mum-of-one filmed the bizarre scenes and shared them on TikTok, where the clip has racked up more than 192,000 views.



Annie, from Hull, East Yorkshire, said: “We thought if we’re going to go to Benidorm, we might as well see what the Benidorm hotel is like.

“We arrived there at 11.30am and there were no beds but obviously at that point we just thought it was because it was midday.

“The next morning, I started seeing queues starting at 6.30am, at this point I didn’t even know what time the pool even opened.

“We had gone down to go and get a latte and there were just loads of people all lining up.

“I can’t believe that’s how you spend your holiday, it’s crazy.



“You see them go, put a towel on the bed then run off straight to the breakfast then eat the breakfast then run straight back. It was a whole routine.

“What we realised was either wives were sending their husbands or the husbands were just doing it because so many of the line was made up of middle-aged men.

“It was just like a sea of people.”



Annie said the only escape from the sunbed scrum was waiting until around 5pm, when holidaymakers began heading out for their evening meals.

Until then, her family had little choice but to use plastic chairs when they were not swimming or playing in the pool.

She said: “You can just go sit at a table and obviously I’ve got a child so we’re always in the pool anyway so I don’t really get much sunbathing.

“It was funny but then about 5pm, people would obviously go out for tea because then the beds would start becoming available and that was the only time without getting in that queue that you could get a bed.

“It’s selfish. Maybe do it one or two times so you can get a spot or have a day on the sunbeds, but there was one woman and she was at the front every single day.



“They [people queueing] were speed walking and as soon as the guy would come down and open the barrier, it was like ants.

“It [the video] caused uproar, I didn’t expect people to get so angry about Benidorm

“Benidorm divides the UK it’s like Marmite, you either love it or you hate it.”

The Benidorm sunbed row sparked a furious reaction online, with some viewers saying they would rather holiday elsewhere.

One wrote: “My idea of hell this is.”



RECOMMENDED STORIES

Another commented: “I’d rather go to Blackpool in the winter.”

A third added: “I love Benidorm but I would never lose sleep when [there’s so much more you can do in Benidorm.”

News.title: Nearly 2,000 prison cells are ‘sitting empty over health & safety risks’ – despite thousands of lags being freed early
News.content:
EMPTY CELLS Nearly 2,000 prison cells are ‘sitting empty over health & safety risks’ – despite thousands of lags being freed early

ALMOST 2,000 prison cells are sitting empty due to health and safety risks despite thousands of lags being freed early.

The prison service has reportedly been force to put cells out of service and move offenders after regulators flagged fire risks.



Up to 1,800 cells currently remain empty as the prison service scrambles to install automatic fire detection (AFD) systems in all cells by 2027, reports The Telegraph.

According to the outlet, around 19,000 cells still require the upgrades as PM Andy Burnham races to find spare capacity in UK prisons and block PC Harper’s killers from an early release.



Government officials have reportedly pledged to install fire safety systems in 10,000 prison cells by 2027 but no date has been set for when the remainder of the work will be carried out.

Chairman of the Prison Officers’ Association, Mark Fairhurst, told The Telegraph that some of the works may be postponed to bring cells into use.



“They have that option. The issue is the safety of the person occupying that cell that has been identified as an imminent fire risk,” he said.

Meanwhile, Gemma Abbott, the legal director of the Howard League for Penal Reform, said it had been “two decades since the government first acknowledged the fire safety shortcomings” in prisons.

In that time, she said that there had been “nine-fire related deaths in public prisons since then”.

She said: “Whilst the chaos of the implementation of the Sentencing Act has understandably drawn attention and ire from across the board, we cannot forget that many of those who remain locked up in prison – and the staff who work there – are being exposed to intolerable fire safety risk.”



A Ministry of Justice spokesperson said: “We take the safety of our prisons extremely seriously and are carrying out these essential fire safety works as quickly as possible.

“This is part of our plan to ensure that we can put more dangerous criminals behind bars and the country never runs out of prison space again.”

Under the new Sentencing Act, which received royal assent in January, a swathe of prisoners were set to be released from September in a bid to ease overcrowding, sparking nationwide outrage.

However, the new PM paused the scheme last month as he ordered a major Ministry of Justice (MoJ) review to identify any grooming gang members who could be eligible for early release.

But it is set to resume instead on October 1 – with thousands of sex offenders, domestic abusers and killers still to see their sentences drastically reduced by two thirds.



It comes as every single police chief in the UK signed a letter urging Mr Burnham to use “every lawful option” to keep PC Andrew Harper’s killers behind bars.

The chiefs expressed their alarm over the impact changes to the release policy could have on confidence in the justice system, policing and public protection.

Albert Bowers and Jessie Cole were jailed for 13 years in 2020 for the manslaughter of 28-year-old officer.

The pair, who were 17 at the time of the offense in August 2019, were passengers in the car that dragged PC Harper for more than a mile along country roads in Berkshire when his ankles got caught in a towrope loop.

After days of confusion and mounting pressure on the government, the PM said there is “more to be done” and he is “turning over every stone”.



The government previously claimed it would reportedly face legal challenges if it tried to block the release of the killers halfway through their jail terms.

After halting the release of over a 1,000 rapists and child sex offenders last week, Burnham said he had reached “the limits” of his intervention powers.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

But on Monday night, a government spokesperson said the PM had asked the Justice Secretary to consider “further options” to keep more serious offenders – including Andrew’s killers – locked up.

The Sun reported on Wednesday how he told PC Harper’s sister that he “wouldn’t forgive himself” if he didn’t try to keep the cop’s killers in prison.

News.title: Sick ISIS video, ‘escape’ to Iran & eerie ‘sightings’… the 14-year mystery of US veteran Austin Tice’s kidnap in Syria
News.content:
AT the height of the Syrian civil war, US Marine Corps veteran and award-winning journalist Austin Tice was abducted just miles from the safety of the Lebanese border.

Austin, then a law student, had spent the summer in the war-torn nation documenting the horrors of Bashar Al-Assad’s brutal crackdown. Now, 14 years later, the fate of the longest captive American journalist in history continues to puzzle investigators.



He vanished three days after his birthday, on August 13, 2012.

Austin had entered Syria in May and travelled through rebel-held areas, freelancing for The Washington Post and McClatchy.



Chilling documents recovered after the fall of Assad’s regime reveal that he was being tracked all the way.

By August, he was getting ready to leave the Syrian capital, Damascus, and travel to Lebanon.

While passing through a checkpoint near Darayya, a southwestern suburb of the city, he vanished.

Then, after around seven weeks of silence, a distressing video emerged with the title “Austin Tice is Alive”.

It showed the journalist blindfolded, bound at the hands, and being led up a rocky hillside by his armed, masked captors who shout “Allahu Akbar”.

A visibly distressed Austin is then forced to recite an Islamic prayer in Arabic.



It is the last-known recording of Austin, who would have turned 44-years-old on Tuesday.

A massive international effort to secure his release has followed in the years since, but has led to far more questions than answers.

For years, the identities of Austin’s captors remained one of the central unanswered questions.



The mysterious video released by his captors seems to suggest that they were Islamic militants, given the religious garb, mountainous geography, and repeated refrains of “Allahu Akbar”.

But US intelligence came to believe that the video had been staged to throw them off the scent.

Analysts noted that the captors wore clothing reminiscent of militants in Afghanistan rather than those operating in Syria at the time.

Elizabeth O’Bagy, an analyst at the Institute for the Study of War, told CBS that the prayers felt forced and appeared to mimic – “in a very poor manner” – those heard in video clips of Afghan fighters.



The clip also appeared on the Facebook page of Assad’s supporters, rather than being routed through the standard jihadist channels.

One of the most extraordinary revelations in recent years is that the journalist may have briefly escaped.

US officials claim that he managed to break out of a hellish Syrian prison shortly after his abduction, before being recaptured by Assad’s henchmen.

Brave Austin reportedly ran through the streets of Damascus in torn clothing after his incredible escape.



Locals in the Mezzeh area, close to where he was abducted, spotted a mysterious man wandering the streets.

Syrian officials released an internal tracking bulletin with Austin’s photo saying that he was at large.

However, he then sought help at the home of a regime figurehead, a senior Syrian official said.



In an extraordinary stroke of bad luck, Austin is said to have knocked on the door of Ali Mamlouk, Assad’s top spook.

He was reportedly swiftly recaptured.

After the fall of Assad’s regime on December 8, 2024, reporters from the Syrian Investigative Reporting for Accountability Journalism (SIRAJ) found top secret intelligence files.

Bombshell documents dated March 4, 2013, reveal that Assad’s security services were meticulously tracking foreign journalists entering the country and covering the civil war.

Austin Tice is named in the file, which suggests that he was still alive at the time, but there are no details of his whereabouts.



His entry reportedly reads: “He entered Syria illegally at the Turkish border in mid-June and he spent several days in Khan Shaikhoun where he met individuals who call themselves the Free Army.”

Reports about Austin’s condition in the years since 2012 have been scarce.

One of the most recent accounts came from a former prisoner interviewed by SIRAJ.

He claimed that he was detained by Syrian spooks in 2018 and held in a cell next to a man who guards would refer to as Austin.

The unnamed man said that he didn’t know who the journalist was at the time.



But he recalled that guards would bring an English translator to speak to the prisoner.

He said: “The translator would ask him, “Austin, what do you want to eat today?’ I could hear the translator talking to Austin directly, because I was close to his cell.”

The story has not been confirmed by official sources, but if true, it would mean he was alive at least six years after his capture.



Last year, a high-ranking general under Assad made the bombshell claim that Austin had been killed back in 2013.

Bassam al-Hassan told CNN: “Of course, Austin is dead,” and claimed that the dictator had personally ordered his execution.

He continued: “I don’t want to protect Bashar al-Assad because he abandoned and left us.

“I don’t want to protect Russia or Iran, because the US thinks Russia and Iran have something to do with the case.

“And I can assure you that this is not the case. This relates to President Bashar only.”



Hassan claimed that he personally passed on the execution order to a member of the National Defense Forces (NDF).

However his claims remain unverified, and CNN reported that the former general failed an FBI-administered polygraph test, and that his account diverges from multiple others.

Sara Qudah, Regional Director of The Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ), said: “Reports that journalist Austin Tice was executed in 2013 are horrifying and demand immediate answers.

“Tice’s family has endured more than a decade of unbearable grief and ambiguous loss.



“CPJ urges United States and Syrian authorities to break their silence, disclose the full truth, and finally provide closure. Accountability cannot be delayed any longer.”

When Assad’s regime was toppled, then-President Joe Biden said the US believed Austin Tice was still alive and would try to bring him home.

He said: “We are mindful that there are Americans in Syria, including those who reside there, as well as Austin Tice, who was taken captive more than 12 years ago.

“We remain committed to returning him to his family.



“We believe he’s alive. We think we can get him back, but we have no direct evidence of that yet. We have to identify where he is.”

Later that month, Biden’s top hostage official Roger Carstens travelled to Damascus to make the first face-to-face contact with the caretaker government and ask for help locating Austin.

The Special Presidential Envoy for Hostage Affairs said he conducted a joint search of a facility with the rebel group that overthrew Assad “that we all thought would have some relation to Austin Tice”.

Carstens told CBS: “We had a lot of information over the last 12 years that pointed to a variety of facilities.

“And in [narrowing] that down over 12 years, we came up with a priority list of about six sites.



“And of those six sites, we felt that this had the highest probability of having held Austin at one time.”

Carstens admitted he was stunned by the sheer number of prisons that Assad had been operating.

He said: “I mean, you’d almost think that if you were running a country, and you wanted to jail your enemies, you’d have one prison, and it wouldn’t be secret.



“But to have like 35 or 40 secret prisons, I find that just horrifying, disturbing, and yet in a way fascinating.”

The diplomatic mission would ultimately return without definitive proof that Austin is still alive.

Despite the so-far unsuccessful attempts to track him down, Austin’s family believe that he may be in the hands of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).

Throughout the civil war, Tehran provided billions of dollars and proxy militias to help prop up the Assad regime.

The IRGC also set up, supervised and controlled secret prisons across Syria during the civil war.



Naomi Tice, one of Austin’s sisters, said that the family has information that he might have been held in one of the facilities and transferred to Iran when Assad was toppled.

She said: “Assad consistently said that he did not have Austin, and he has really held strong on that message.

“We also know that Iran manages some of the detention facilities in Syria.

“And so, that technicality could be one of the reasons why Assad said that he didn’t have them because Iran was technically in control of them at the time.”

“With the regime change, we do think, at that point, Austin might have been brought over to Iran during that time.



“Once again, this isn’t confirmed, but we have strong reason to believe that might be the case.”

The family has urged Donald Trump‘s administration to ask for information about Austin’s whereabouts as part of negotiations to bring an end to the war.

Assad, who was recently sentenced to death in absentia, is currently exiled in Moscow.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

The Tice family has urged Washington to put pressure on Vladimir Putin so that the deposed dictator can be questioned by US investigators.

But 14 years on, there remains limited information about the missing journalist.

News.title: Pero's bridge 'collapses' in Bristol harbour in front of stunned onlookers
News.content:
Pero's bridge 'collapses' in Bristol harbour in front of stunned onlookers

Pero's footbridge spanning Bristol's floating harbour has been closed after witnesses described it 'collapsing' in front of them this morning

View 3 Images The incident occurred in Bristol this morning (Image: Submitted)

A bridge in Bristol has been closed after it 'collapsed' this morning.

‌



Witnesses describe hearing a 'crack' before seeing Pero's footbridge - which spans St Augustine's Reach in Bristol harbour - 'come down'.

‌



Photos and videos show a barrier closing off the pathway as well as a clear break in the bridge. Thankfully, it doesn't appear as if anyone was on the bridge at the time.

‌



Bristol City Council is yet to confirm exactly what happened.

One witness told Bristol Live: "Pero's bridge (City Centre) just failed its maintenance check and now the middle is hanging into the harbour."

View 3 Images The bridge has since been blocked off (Image: Submitted)

‌



Criminal probe launched as pilot and student die in 'disturbing' Essex plane crash READ MORE :

Another said: "I arrived just as a fence was being put across blocking people and there was a lady next to me saying it had collapsed right in front of her and had only just happened."

And a third said: "We were at the V-Shed heard what sounded like a crack, looked up and could see it come crashing down. No person was on the bridge at the time and engineers [seemed] to be testing it.

"It didn’t come down fast as it was under the hydraulic pressure which I believe failed causing it to come down!"

‌



View 3 Images Witnesses describe hearing a 'crack (Image: Submitted)

Council and harbour authority staff are at the scene, both on land and in a boat looking at the underside of bridge.

Bristol City Council announced in June 2025 that three tonnes of padlocks attached to the footbridge were to be removed.

Article continues below

Locks were removed by the council over a decade ago, but people then attached new ones and the bridge was covered again within a few years.

The bridge opened in 1999 and was named after Pero Jones, who was enslaved and lived in Bristol in the 18th century.

News.title: 'I tried the weirdest heatwave home cooling method and it worked'
News.content:
'I tried the weirdest heatwave home cooling method and it worked'

Civil engineer Emma Kent tested the bizarre technique and says it actually works

View 3 Images Emma Kent

A woman who tried a 'fast and cheap' heatwave hack that is said to keep homes cool for several weeks says it works - and doesn't smell as bad as you would think. As the UK suffers through its fifth heatwave this summer, with temperatures potentially hitting 38C, people are searching for ways to keep cool.

‌



Emma Kent has taken to using a rather bizarre hack to beat the heat. It involves painting each window with Greek yoghurt. “The yoghurt doesn’t actually cool the home, per se,” said the civil engineer, from Hitchin. “But when painted on outside of the windows, the yoghurt prevents sunlight from entering and therefore stops your home from heating up.

‌



“I noticed the results the next day after we had cooled the house down overnight. And then it helped prevent heat gain immediately."

‌



View 3 Images You fill a paint tray with yogurt and apply it with a roller

The 42-year-old says it made a 1.5C difference in the top-floor room where it was painted, as well as reducing solar glare and discomfort from the sunshine. She suggests applying it once and then leaving it to dry into a hard layer, which should last until it’s washed off – or up to several weeks.

‌



It takes just five minutes and costs only £2.50. T he hack was found on the website Heatwave Toolkit.

Emma was happy to test it out – and says it’s a winner. She added, “It smelled for about two minutes, then dried into an opaque, hard paste, with no smell. There were no files or any of the issues you might imagine.

View 3 Images You paint the glass with yogurt

Article continues below

“I did feel a bit silly getting the decorating gear out, then filling a paint tray with yoghurt. But I trusted in the process. I was glad I did it as it worked well.

“The window cleaner came round soon after my first batch, and it washed off easily, so I chose to reapply it. Obviously it’s a cheap, quick fix and external shading such as shutters, blinds or shade sails would be more effective.”

News.title: House designed by Isambard Kingdom Brunel goes on the market for £4m
News.content:
House designed by Isambard Kingdom Brunel goes on the market for £4m

A stunning Grade II-listed mansion that was commissioned by the engineer Isambard Kingdom Brunel has been listed with planning permission for more homes to be built

View 4 Images A mansion designed by Isambard Kingdom Brunel for his retirement is up for sale (Image: Savills / SWNS)

The Grade II-listed mansion where Isambard Kingdom Brunel had planned to spend his retirement has gone on sale for £4million.

‌



The engineer had commissioned the grand property in Torquay, Devon, but he died in 1859 before having the chance to live at the property. The home is now on the market for £4million – but comes with planning permission to construct a further 35 homes.

‌



The huge site, which sits on over ten acres of land, is currently divided into three separate properties: Brunel Manor, Brunel Court and Brunel Lodge. Brunel Manor, built over four storeys, is fitted with six reception rooms and 55 bedrooms.

‌



View 4 Images The property comes with 10 acres of land (Image: Savills / SWNS)

Brunel Court, the former stable block to the main house, was converted into three cottages and a flat. The third building, Brunel Lodge, had three reception rooms and nine bedrooms.

ATA Estates acquired the remainder of the estate, roughly five years ago, from the Woodlands House of Prayer, a charity that had operated the property as a hotel and Christian retreat and conference centre.

‌



Following extensive consultations with Historic England, the Torbay Design Review Panel and the local authority, Torbay Council granted planning permission for the project in June 2025.

View 4 Images The mansion has been listed for £4million (Image: Savills / SWNS)

The plans involve demolishing the modern extensions to restore the setting of the listed buildings, converting them into 26 apartments and homes. Nine newly built properties will also be erected on the site.

‌



ATA Estates say they have considered all avenues including a potential sale but, having fallen head over heels for the project, they are intent on pressing ahead themselves should no buyer come forward. They are aiming to break ground on construction in the new year. The property is listed with Savills and offers will be considered throughout the process.

View 4 Images Isambard Kingdom Brunel died before he was able to live in his retirement home (Image: Getty Images)

Andy Fudge, who has been spearheading the project, said: "As part of our investigations, before even considering potential options for the site, we carried out detailed research into the history of the property and grounds and it was immediately apparent there was a fascinating history to the estate due to its connection to Isambard Kingdom Brunel, which in his time extended to some 600 acres.

Article continues below

"It was an absolute tragedy that Brunel never got to live there himself as he passed away before construction reached above foundation level.

"But, from our investigations, it was apparent the site deserved to be treated with the utmost respect and approached from a 'heritage first' perspective to ensure its survival going forwards did not detract from its previous storied history.

"We are excited to have reached the next stage of its restoration and redevelopment and for the next evolution in the life of Brunel Manor to commence."

News.title: Stone Roses' Mani's £1million home up for sale after family's emotional farewell
News.content:
Stone Roses' Mani's £1million home up for sale after family's emotional farewell

The five-bedroom home near Heaton Moor, Greater Manchester once lived in by the Stone Roses legend and his wife Imelda has gone on sale for over £1million

View 5 Images Stone Roses bassist Mani died last year at the age of 63 (Image: SWNS)

Stone Roses legend Gary 'Mani' Mounfield's home has gone on the market for over £1million after his brother-in-law said it was 'time to move on'. The five-bedroom property near Heaton Moor, Stockport, Greater Manchester, once lived in by the famous bassist and his family, has been put up for sale.

‌



Mani and his wife Imelda moved into in the semi-detached property in 2014 with their twin sons, and lived there until their deaths.

‌



Imelda passed away after a battle with cancer in 2023, aged 50, and Mani died almost two years later in November 2025 at the age of 63.

‌



According to estate agents John Mellor, the Victorian home, which has three bathrooms, "oozes with the charm and character of its era" while having "modern thinking improvements" such as en-suite bathrooms, a utility area, double glazing and central heating.

Man dead after massive explosion rocks Buckinghamshire village as home destroyed READ MORE :

House designed by Isambard Kingdom Brunel goes on the market for £4m READ MORE :

View 5 Images The 'charming' Victorian property is on the market for £1.05million (Image: John Mellor / SWNS)

It is set behind an electric gate and spread over four floors, including a range of cellar rooms. Mani's brother-in-law Michael Ryder, who is now the guardian of his two 13-year-old boys, says it was a hard decision to sell but that it was time for the family to move on.

‌



View 5 Images The home is set behind an electric gate and spread over four floors (Image: John Mellor / SWNS)

He said: "We had a lot of great memories in the house. There were some good parties there. "It is a lovely house, but life changes. It is time to move on." Mani died in his sleep of respiratory issues following a long battle with emphysema, a chronic lung condition.

View 5 Images Mani's brother-in-law said the family feel it it 'time to move on' and sell the home (Image: John Mellor / SWNS)

‌



Michael said the house is now full of "sad memories" from this time, but that he is certain the new owners will love it. John Mellor have listed the home for a guide price of £1,050,000.

View 5 Images The property boasts en-suite bathrooms, a utility area, double glazing and central heating (Image: John Mellor / SWNS)

The listing reads: "A stunning and most imposing semi detached family home standing on a very generous corner plot with extended accommodation, delightful garden areas and parking to the rear accessed via an electric gate and further benefitting from an EV charger. "The accommodation is generously spread over four floors including a fantastic range of cellar rooms.

Article continues below

"The property oozes with the charm and character of its era, sadly lacking in todays more modern constructions, but does have modern thinking improvements such as en-suite bathrooms, a utility area, double glazing and a modern gas central heating system."

Mani joined the Stone Roses in 1987, with his bass riffs forming an integral part of their self-titled debut album and their follow-up, the Second Coming.

He joined Primal Scream after the group split up in 1996, before returning to his old band for their 2012-13 reunion tour.

News.title: Boy, 7, his cousin, 15, and her mum were on holiday when they died in Mersea Beach tragedy
News.content:
Boy, 7, his cousin, 15, and her mum were on holiday when they died in Mersea Beach tragedy

Musa Ahmed got into difficulty in the water at West Mersea on July 22, his cousin Sameeha Rahman, 15, and her mother Shelina Rahman, 41, also died in the incident

View 2 Images Emergency services swarmed West Mersea beach after the tragic incident (Image: Daniel Rees/Newsquest/SWNS)

A seven-year-old drowned after he suffered a fatal brain injury off an Essex beach while on holiday with his family.

‌



Musa Ahmed got into difficulty in the water in West Mersea on July 22 an inquest heard today. He died in hospital six days later.

‌



His cousin Sameeha Rahman, 15, and her mother Shelina Rahman, 41, both from Ilford in east London, also died in the tragic incident.

‌



The three were in the water along with three other family members - including two adults and one child - when they got into difficulty. All family members made "significant efforts to help each other," police said at the time of the incident.

Sameeha and Shelina Rahman were pronounced dead at the scene, while Musa from Romford in Essex, was brought to shore, stabilised and then flown to the Royal London Hospital. He died there on July 28, the opening of an inquest into the deaths heard on Thursday.

View 2 Images Samiha Rahman, 15, died while trying to save her seven-year-old cousin

‌



The hearing at Chelmsford County Hall was told the trio had been on a family holiday at the time and that post-mortem examinations had given a provisional cause of death as drowning for all three.

For Musa, hypoxic ischaemic brain injury was also recorded as a provisional cause of death.

Senior coroner for Essex Lincoln Brookes said: “Clearly it is so tragic to come across any death of any individual but when three occur at the same time and of the same family, one cannot underestimate the tragic nature of such an incident.”

‌



Mr Brookes offered his “deepest condolences” to the family, friends and loved ones of the victims.

Essex Police previously said officers were called by the ambulance service at 5.35pm on July 22 after reports that several people had got into difficulty in the water near Seaview Avenue.

The coroner adjourned the inquest to January 19, 2027.

Article continues below

The Mirror has launched the Save Lives For Sam water safety campaign to tackle the UK's growing drowning crisis. Backed by MPs, Olympic champions, national water safety organisations and bereaved families, the campaign is calling for urgent action to make our waters safer.

That includes compulsory water safety lessons in schools, a nationwide public awareness campaign, better lifesaving equipment at high-risk waterways, the introduction of Sam's Law, and a dedicated Minister for Water Safety. Find out more about the campaign and how you can support it here.
