World.title: SEN TOM COTTON: Democrats say socialism will help. History says it will hurt
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Americans are worried about the cost of living — and rightly so. The price of groceries, housing and many everyday necessities rose by roughly 30% under President Biden. While price increases have slowed under Republican leadership, the devastating effects of that inflation remain. Democrats' self-described "socialist" solution — a dramatic expansion of government welfare, regulation and taxation — would make life even more expensive for American families.

History has already run this big government socialist experiment again and again. From Venezuela to Cuba to the Soviet Union, countries that embraced socialism have produced the same results: shortages, inflation, declining investment, fewer opportunities and higher prices for their citizens.

First, look at Venezuela, which has some of the world's largest oil reserves. Venezuela should have been among the wealthiest nations in the Western Hemisphere, but decades of socialist policies — such as nationalizing industry, reckless government spending and sweeping price controls — have devastated its economy, destroyed the currency and skyrocketed inflation.

I WATCHED CHICAGO PROMISE FOOD EQUITY. NOW MY NEIGHBORHOOD HAS EMPTY SHELVES

For years, Venezuelans have paid the price for these failed socialist policies as grocery shelves emptied, basic medicines disappeared and hourslong lines formed for staples like flour and rice. Toilet paper became so scarce that it became an international symbol of Venezuela's collapse. And because of inflation, a loaf of bread that once cost only a few bolívars eventually cost millions.

Also consider Cuba, where state ownership and central planning have similarly failed to generate prosperity and provide food for its people, despite having fertile agricultural lands. More than six decades after the communist revolution, Cuba imports as much as 80% of its food, yet Cubans still endure chronic shortages. Ration books remain part of daily life. Buildings crumble. Young people leave whenever they can. Even basic household necessities often require standing in long lines or having personal connections to obtain.

And in the Soviet Union, citizens living behind the Iron Curtain grew accustomed to empty shelves, endless waiting lists and chronic shortages of everything, including butter, meat, shoes, coffee, household appliances and automobiles. Sure, the government-controlled Soviet economy could build shoddy tanks and missiles, but it struggled to provide decent housing, quality consumer goods and reliable food supplies. Bureaucrats simply could not replace the countless daily decisions made by millions of producers, workers, entrepreneurs and consumers operating in competitive markets. The problem wasn't bad management. It was the centralized, top-down system itself.

The lesson is clear: socialism doesn't eliminate scarcity. It creates it. While supporters of socialism often blame sanctions or embargoes for these struggles, in reality, these consequences are the result of socialist policies that never work and always fail.

CAPITALISM IS ABOUT INCENTIVES. STOPPING THE STUPIDITY OF SOCIALISM IS A BIG INCENTIVE

Some also point to Scandinavia as proof the socialist model can succeed. But Denmark, Sweden, Norway and Finland aren’t purely socialist. After all, these nations rely on private enterprise, secure property rights, competitive markets and successful global private companies. Yes, their governments operate larger welfare programs, but those programs are financed by high taxes on ordinary workers — not simply by "taxing billionaires."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

For example, Denmark, Sweden and Norway’s tax-to-GDP ratios top 40%, and all three countries impose a 25% value-added tax on most purchases, increasing costs on pretty much every consumer purchase. Add this to the housing prices, which in cities such as Stockholm, Oslo and Copenhagen rank among the most expensive in Europe, and the Nordic model offers no evidence that an expansive welfare state makes life more affordable for average citizens.

MAMDANI’S CITY GROCERY PLAN COULD LEAVE TAXPAYERS PAYING FOR EVERY BANANA

In America, socialist ideas championed by the likes of New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson, Senator Bernie Sanders and Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez are no longer confined to college seminars or political fringes. Self-described democratic socialists — many of whom have never experienced socialism firsthand — have won major primaries, secured seats in Congress and influenced the Democratic Party's agenda. Proposals once considered politically impossible — such as government-owned grocery stores, universal rent control and greater government management of the economy — are now mainstream.

History offers a warning that should not be ignored. America's strength has always rested on the hard work and ingenuity of its people, not the commands of socialist bureaucracies. Wherever socialism has expanded government control over the economy, ordinary citizens have paid the price through higher costs, fewer choices and declining prosperity.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Americans shouldn't be forced to learn that lesson the hard way. They should remember it before casting their next vote.

Because socialism doesn't make life cheaper. It makes life more expensive.

World.title: College students express strong trust in school leaders despite broader public cynicism: Gallup
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

FIRST ON FOX — Most college students hold a positive view of their institution’s leadership — in stark contrast with the general American public’s declining trust in higher education, according to a new Gallup poll exclusively obtained by Fox News Digital.

"Recent Lumina-Gallup research finds that college students’ experience contradicts many of the concerns raised by U.S. adults who lack confidence in higher education," the report stated.

"By wide margins, both currently enrolled students and graduates agree that their degree is or has been worth the cost and is important to their career success," the survey explained. "However, while students remain confident in the value of their degree, more than four in 10 also question whether the college or university they are attending consistently acts in their best interests."

FOX NEWS POLL: FAITH IN HIGHER EDUCATION IN THE US IS COLLAPSING

The poll, joint-conducted by the Lumina Foundation and Gallup, found that 55% of college students believe their school’s administration usually makes decisions with students' best interests in mind.

According to the findings, 12% of students say leadership acts in their best interest "all of the time," while 43% say "most of the time." Meanwhile, about one in three students (35%) say their school acts in their interest "some of the time," with roughly one in 10 saying leadership "rarely" (9%) or "never" (2%) does.

The survey revealed that students attending top-tier institutions — as ranked by U.S. News & World Report — are slightly less likely to believe their school prioritizes their interests. Despite this, students across the board expressed significantly higher confidence in campus leadership than in elected political officials.

The findings were based on a survey of 3,801 currently enrolled associate and bachelor’s degree students between the ages of 18 and 59, conducted Oct. 2–31.

LIZ PEEK: TRUMP IS STARVING THE MACHINE THAT CREATES AMERICA'S SOCIALIST REVOLUTIONARIES

The data comes on the heels of broader Gallup polling that showed public confidence in U.S. higher education dropping back down, erasing a brief post-pandemic recovery as concerns over campus politics, rising tuition and degree value intensify.

Just 38% of U.S. adults currently maintain a "great deal" or "quite a lot" of confidence in higher education. That figure marks a noticeable dip from last year, when public trust briefly bounced to 42%.

"It's kind of the three things that we see — those are still front and center as to why people aren't as confident in higher ed as they used to be: the cost, the perception that there's a political agenda being taught, and the perception that they're not teaching people the right kinds of things they need to succeed in the job once they finish," a Gallup expert told Fox News Digital in an interview.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

The findings arrive amid an intensified effort by federal lawmakers and conservative advocates targeting viewpoint discrimination, antisemitism, and diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) frameworks across American universities.

World.title: 5-step sleep reset could promote healthy weight loss, nutritionist says
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

One weekly routine could help foster better sleep and promote healthy weight loss, according to a New Jersey-based registered dietitian.

Erin Palinski-Wade, who is also a certified diabetes care specialist and author of "The Sleepdemic Solution," shared her "seven-day reset" in an interview with Fox News Digital.

The reset combines sleep, nutrition and lifestyle strategies into a five-part system represented by the acronym SLEEP.

SKIPPING SLEEP MAY PACK ON POUNDS FASTER THAN YOU THINK, NEW STUDY FINDS

In a test panel conducted in connection with her seven-day program, Palinski-Wade said participants reported improvements in sleep, blood sugar and weight.

Experts recommend consulting a healthcare professional for individualized guidance before making significant changes to diet, sleep or lifestyle habits, particularly for those with underlying health conditions.

POPULAR WEIGHT-LOSS DRUGS MAY HELP PROTECT AGAINST A DEADLY DISEASE, DOCTOR SAYS

Palinski-Wade emphasized that results varied among participants with different sleep challenges. The panel included shift workers, mothers and people with long-term insomnia.

Despite those differences, within the first two to three days, the expert said people "across the board" reported falling asleep faster, getting higher-quality sleep and feeling more rested the next day.

Panelists with pre-existing insulin resistance or type 2 diabetes also reported improvements in blood sugar levels, Palinski-Wade said.

"Once they were resting better and those stress hormones were reduced, and the body was getting the rest it needed, we were seeing better balanced blood sugar throughout the day," she noted.

Participants also reported improvements in hunger and satiety.

DOCTORS SAY 8 FORGOTTEN HABITS COULD HELP FIGHT STRESS, OBESITY AND CHRONIC DISEASE

"They weren't having those cravings, especially in the evening, especially those sugar cravings," Palinski-Wade said. "When they were eating, they were feeling more satisfied."

"I had a few test panel members who lost as much as seven pounds in the first seven days," she said, noting that some of the loss was water weight.

Participants reported reductions in weight and waist circumference and improvements in blood sugar, sleep and next-day energy.

The Reset

Below, Palinski-Wade breaks down the five components of the SLEEP system.

S – Set your rhythm

Setting a rhythm involves timing meals consistently to help improve sleep. This means avoiding skipped meals, which can lead to blood sugar fluctuations throughout the day, Palinski-Wade said.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

"We want to be fueling our body all throughout the day so that our body is expecting to sleep in the evening," she said.

Skipping meals and consuming excess food and calories in the evening tells the body that it's time to burn energy, which is not going to be conducive to sleep, according to the expert.

L – Leveraging light

Exposure to sunlight within the first hour of waking can help set the body’s circadian rhythm, Palinski-Wade noted.

"When your body gets that natural light, whether you go outside or put your desk by the window, that's helping your body get more in tune with that rhythm where you're awake," she said.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

In the evening, Palinski-Wade recommends dimming the lights and avoiding electronics and bright overhead lighting, which helps the body wind down and prepare for restful sleep.

E – Eat with intention

Eating with intention means choosing meals and snacks with nutrients that support healthy sleep, according to Palinski-Wade.

CLICK HERE TO 

"Whether it's serotonin and tryptophan, anti-inflammatory nutrients, we want to make sure that we're eating with intention, so we're giving our body the building blocks it needs to create sleep in the evening," she said.

E – Evening out blood sugar

Palinski-Wade recommends combining lean protein, healthy fats and fiber to help keep blood sugar steady throughout the day and support better sleep.

P – Powering down your night

Powering down involves creating a consistent nighttime routine, including limiting electronics and caffeine and maintaining regular sleep and wake times, according to Palinski-Wade.

"That also applies to having a set bedtime and a set wake time ... in those seven days to reset that circadian rhythm, so we can have the best results moving forward," she said.

"We want to be fueling our body all throughout the day so that our body is expecting to sleep in the evening."

For those who are "trying everything," like diet and exercise, without seeing results, Palinski-Wade stressed that it is "not because you don’t have enough willpower."

"It could just be your biology working against you, and many times it's as simple as improving your sleep," she said. "If you start to improve your sleep within just a few days, you can see major changes in how you feel, how your body is processing food, in your metabolism, and then ultimately in your body weight."

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

External research by the National Institutes of Health has also linked adequate sleep with appetite regulation and healthy weight management.

The National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute states that sleep helps regulate hormones involved in hunger and fullness, while sleep deficiency can affect the body's response to insulin and has been linked to a higher risk of obesity.

World.title: Comedian declares Hugh Laurie 'can't be canceled' as actor comes to Sophie Cunningham's defense
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Golden Globe winner Hugh Laurie rejected the idea of biological men competing in women’s sports this week and voiced his support for WNBA guard Sophie Cunningham.

The comments came during an exchange with comedian Graham Linehan, who pressed Laurie to clarify his views after the actor initially posted a dry observation on X about biological height advantage in professional basketball. Linehan called Laurie’s indirect wording "cowardly" in a now-deleted post, prompting the actor to deliver a blunt response.

Laurie, best known for playing Dr. Gregory House in the hit drama "House," then clarified his position on X. "Firstly, f--- off; secondly no, I don’t believe men should compete against women. I thought I’d made that pretty clear. If you’d looked. But obviously you must get onto your next," he wrote.

SOPHIE CUNNINGHAM SENDS MESSAGE TO HER HATERS AFTER SAYING MEN DON'T BELONG IN WOMEN'S SPORTS

Linehan pressed Laurie further, telling him to "just say that you support Sophie Cunningham in her fight for fair sports and stop trying to be arch." Laurie responded:

"You started it. ‘Cowardly’ to ‘f--- off’ is the going rate of exchange around here. And yes, I support Sophie Cunningham. And you, some of the time," Laurie posted Monday.

Linehan then apologized for his reaction, writing, "Fair dos. I apologise for my knee-jerkiness. And thank you. I would never have had what career I had without 'A Bit Of Fry and Laurie' to aspire towards."

The subsequent X exchange quickly went viral, racking up millions of views as users debated Laurie’s stance. Some criticized the actor for opposing transgender athletes competing in women’s sports, while others praised the Hollywood star for publicly supporting women’s sports.

Comedian and political commentator Tim Young told Fox News Digital that Laurie’s established career gives him more freedom to voice his opinion without fear of being canceled.

"It’s so rare that someone from Hollywood would stand up for women in women’s sports that it’s exciting when someone does at this point. Hugh Laurie aka Dr. House simply said he stood with Sophie Cunningham, and now he gets to see the ugly side of the left for the first time," Young said, adding, "Laurie can’t be canceled."

WHITE HOUSE DEFENDS WNBA STAR SOPHIE CUNNINGHAM AFTER SHE SPEAKS OUT IN SUPPORT OF PROTECTING WOMEN'S SPORTS

Young also argued that financial considerations can influence what performers say publicly: "Comedians always stand at the forefront of social commentary, but many of their opinions come from who pays them. Here we see someone established like Laurie against someone who is afraid of being canceled. I think that’s a heavier factor than anything else."

"Unfortunately, a lot of times, comedians, albeit the loudest among the people, are some of the dumbest, same with actors and musicians, and similar to every other issue, you should side here with common sense, not what the famous guy said," Young said. "This time it just so happens that he’s right and my favorite TV doctor of all time," he added.

LEFT-LEANING COMEDIAN LABELED 'CHILDISH' BY CONSERVATIVE JEFF DYE AFTER INSULT SCRAWLED ON TESLA

The debate over transgender athletes competing in women’s sports has taken center court in the WNBA, where Indiana Fever guard Sophie Cunningham has recently said women and girls should not have to compete against biological men.

Fox News Digital reached out to representatives for Laurie and Linehan but did not immediately hear back.

A former Chicago detective says the Windy City should look to a southern city where murders have plunged since the National Guard members moved in to find a way out of its crime crisis.

President Donald Trump had signed an executive order in September 2025 authorizing the deployment of the National Guard, allowing troops to arrive in Memphis that fall.

On Monday night alone, nine people were shot across Chicago, including three who were killed. In one incident, two men were critically injured after gunfire rang out in the city's Near North Side neighborhood.

CHICAGO OFFICERS WOUNDED IN TRAFFIC STOP SHOOTOUT AS HOLIDAY WEEKEND LEAVES 3 DEAD, 16 INJURED

"When we were in our living room, and we thought that another sporadic rainstorm hit Chicago, so we go outside in the windows, next thing you know, we just hear like lights everywhere," one person told FOX 32.

"Chicago has just 2,500 fewer police officers than it did just two or three years ago. You can't keep doing more with less. It's got to come down," Roy said. MEMPHIS PIZZA JOINT SPARKS BACKLASH AFTER OWNER REFUSES TO SERVE NATIONAL GUARD TROOPS

"The mere presence of police serves as a disincentive to commit crime. You want people to say, 'hey, people are going out to do something, a robbery, a burglary or whatever. Man, it's hot out here. World.title: Single ticket bought in Illinois wins $1 billion Powerball jackpot
World.content:
To the tens of thousands and likely more dreaming about a $1 billion Powerball win, the anticipation is over: Someone who bought a ticket in Illinois won it all.

A single ticket sold in the state matched all six numbers and the Powerball to win Wednesday’s $1.04 billion jackpot, which is the eighth largest in the history of the lottery game, organizers said.

The winning numbers were 4, 26, 66, 67 and 69, with a Powerball of 9.

If it is taken all at once as a lump-sum payment, the jackpot is $450.5 million before taxes. Otherwise, it would be an annuity paid out over 29 years.

A jackpot of $1 billion was once extraordinary, but the game has made changes to increase the amount in the top prize.

The biggest one so far was the $2.04 billion jackpot won in 2022, and the second and third biggest — $1.817 billion and $1.787 billion — were both won last year.

The last time someone won the Powerball jackpot was May 2. When no one wins, the jackpot rolls over and increases. Once someone wins, it resets to a default $20 million.

The game recently expanded to allow bettors in the United Kingdom to participate. That started July 21.

In the U.S., it’s played in 45 states, the District of Columbia, Puerto Rico and the U.S. Virgin Islands.

World.title: Army gynecologist pleads not guilty to secretly recording patients
World.content:
An Army gynecologist charged with secretly video recording patients during exams pleaded not guilty Wednesday.

Dr. Blaine McGraw is charged with indecent visual recording, as well as conduct unbecoming of an officer, willful disobedience of a superior officer and making a false statement. The Army Office of Special Trial Counsel previously alleged that there were 44 victims throughout 2025. McGraw’s patients included hundreds of service members and their spouses.

McGraw appeared before Col. Jorge Rivera, a military judge, at the Lawrence Williams Judicial Center at Fort Hood, Texas, on Wednesday, according to NBC affiliate KCEN of Temple.

According to information presented in court Wednesday, McGraw now faces nine charges and 273 specifications involving 93 alleged victims, the station reported. The Army has said the alleged conduct occurred from 2021 to 2026.

The specifications include 12 of sexual assault, 79 of attempted sexual assault, 66 of indecent recording and 91 of assault consummated by a battery, KCEN reported.

He was charged in December after the Army Criminal Investigation Division opened an inquiry in October following a complaint from a patient at Fort Hood. Most of the accusations are related to medical exams of female patients at the Carl R. Darnall Army Medical Center at Fort Hood, where he worked.

Blaine McGraw. Bell County Sheriff's Office

NBC News was first to report details of the allegations against McGraw, including an interview with a former patient who sued him after having learned he had recorded “nearly the entirety of her final appointment, including both the breast and pelvic examinations, without her knowledge or consent,” her lawsuit says.

Her lawsuit alleges that there are scores of additional victims and that Army leadership allowed McGraw to continue practicing for years after it received complaints about sexual misconduct — an allegation the Army denies. She is married to an active-duty service member and sued anonymously, using the name Jane Doe, to keep her identity private.

Fort Hood officials have said they immediately suspended McGraw and opened an investigation after they received the complaint in October. The commander at Darnall Army Medical Center told NBC News in November that he had identified more than 1,400 of McGraw’s patients to inform of the investigation.

McGraw also worked at Tripler Army Medical Center in Hawaii from June 2019 to June 2023. The Army notified his former patients there about the investigation and how to report any complaints, NBC News reported.

If you or someone you know has been sexually assaulted, call the National Sexual Assault Hotline at 1-800-656-4673. The hotline, run by the Rape, Abuse, & Incest National Network (RAINN), can put you in contact with your local rape crisis center. You can also access RAINN’s online chat service at rainn.org/get-help.

World.title: Pardoned Jan. 6 defendant convicted in ‘creepy’ hair-touching case
World.content:
A pardoned Jan. 6 defendant was found guilty Wednesday of a single count of simple assault for sitting behind a woman on a train, touching her hair and posting the incident to social media.

Bryan Betancur, of Silver Spring, Maryland, was found guilty in Washington, D.C., Superior Court of surreptitiously fondling a woman’s hair on a Metro Red Line train in February.

“It’s just a creepy thing to do,” the judge said in court.

The victim identified in the video also spoke in court, saying, “I think about this video every single day. I think about this video every time I get on the Metro, which is twice every single day.”

She said it’s changed how she feels about being in public and that she feels paranoid and exposed after the incident.

“It was very upsetting and unsettling to see someone had touched me and posted about it on the internet without my consent,” she testified.

The maximum sentence for the charge, which is a misdemeanor, is 180 days. Betancur has already served 125 days after a judge ordered him held in custody in April over an alleged bail violation.

Bryan Betancur displays his certificate of pardon from President Donald Trump at a Jan. 6 memorial march in Washington this year. Chip Somodevilla / Getty Images file

Prosecutors indicated they would argue for more jail time, rather than giving Betancur credit for time served. In addition to jail time, he could receive a $1,000 fine.

A sentencing hearing is set for Thursday afternoon.

Betancur is also facing a stalking charge in Washington, D.C., and an additional assault and battery charge in Arlington, Virginia. The Arlington charge stems from an incident similar to the one he was convicted of Wednesday: He is accused of livestreaming himself fondling the hair of a different woman on a train there.

The FBI has said Betancur is a self-professed white supremacist, who was photographed holding a Confederate flag during the Jan. 6 insurrection.

It was part of a federal case against Betancur in which the FBI said he was on parole for burglary charges and wearing an ankle monitor while taking part in the insurrection of the Capitol. He was sentenced to jail but was later pardoned by President Donald Trump.

Swampy underarms are a common symptom of summer heat, and to combat it, you need a strong deodorant or antiperspirant. Aluminum deodorants, also known as antiperspirant deodorants, are a great option for anyone dealing with excessive sweat and stubborn body odor, since they do the double-duty of reducing odor and helping to block sweat glands, which reduces perspiration and odor-causing bacteria overall. While not all deodorants stop sweat, all aluminum deodorants are antiperspirants as well, since they include aluminum salts, which is the key ingredient used for blocking sweat in antiperspirants.

Although aluminum formulas have drawn scrutiny in the past for perceived links to cancer, particularly breast cancer, it’s important to note that the fears aren’t exactly based in fact. According to the American Cancer Society, there is no strong scientific evidence to prove the link between aluminum and cancer in deodorants, maintaining it as a safe option for underarm sweat prevention.

World.title: Democratic senators demand answers about conditions aboard USS Abraham Lincoln
World.content:
Washington — Senate Democrats demanded answers Wednesday about conditions aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln, following reports of food shortages, broken plumbing and mental health crises during the aircraft carrier's record-setting deployment.

In a letter to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao, Sen. Richard Blumenthal, of Connecticut, called for the Navy to account for conditions aboard the carrier, which he said "has been deployed more than 250 days" without coming ashore "in over 200 days, setting a record for consecutive days at sea."

Blumenthal voiced concern over such extended deployments, noting "widespread reports of shortages of basic supplies, water contamination, plumbing issues, deteriorating mental health, deck safety concerns" and other problems aboard the Lincoln.

A Navy official told CBS News that the "Lincoln is operating in a highly contested environment where traditional supply hubs in the Middle East were disrupted by combat actions. In response, leadership prioritized mission-critical supplies: first food, then hygiene items, then mail. Current reports from the ship confirm continuous access to clean water, functional AC, and healthy meal options."

The carrier departed San Diego on Nov. 21 last year for duty in the South China Sea and was rerouted to the Middle East before U.S.-Israeli attacks on Iran began on Feb. 28.

In two recent meetings, family members clashed with Navy leadership over the difficult conditions — including food shortages — faced by the 5,000 sailors and Marines aboard the Lincoln and demanded to know when loved ones would return home, MSNOW reported.

Some families reported severe mental health issues and attempted suicides on board.

Citing a report in the Military Times that several sailors had tried to jump overboard or were prevented from trying to in recent months, Sen. Ruben Gallego, of Arizona, said in a social media post Wednesday that the Navy "must allow a bipartisan Congressional Delegation to visit the USS Lincoln to conduct (an) oversight investigation into this horrible situation."

The Navy official told CBS News,"Based on information available to the command, we have not identified an increase in reported suicidal ideation or suicide attempts aboard the ship. ... (The) Lincoln is providing a comprehensive support network, including onboard deployment-resilience counselors, chaplains, Fleet and Family Support Center services, Military OneSource, and medical professionals."

World.title: Police seize 1,000 pounds of cocaine with stickers of soccer star
World.content:
Norway's soccer star Erling Haaland's face has appeared on billboards, trading cards and television screens, becoming a social media phenomenon for scoring seven goals across four World Cup matches in July.

Now, police in Ecuador have found it in an unexpected place — printed on green rectangular packages that made up a stunning cocaine shipment seized in a truck near the Colombian border.

The driver of the vehicle was arrested following the seizure of the stash of 469 kilograms (1,034 pounds) of cocaine on Wednesday, police said in a statement.

A news release said anti-narcotics agents were conducting an operation following an anonymous tip received early Tuesday morning on the Pan-American Highway when they noticed a suspicious truck. After searching it, they found 370 packages hidden in a false bottom of the truck.

Police released a video showing the packages spilling out from the truck's false bottom, with the stickers of Haaland — often called a "pretty princess" and "babygirl" by his fans — clearly visible.

This image from a video released by Ecuador National Police shows alleged bricks of cocaine which Ecuadorian police removed from a truck in Carchi, Ecuador, Aug. 12, 2026. Ecuador National Police via AP

Haaland was one of the top scorers and most charismatic players at the World Cup held in Mexico, the United States and Canada, and his imposing stature, goofy sense of humor and seemingly endless appetite sparked a wave of creative viral videos and memes.

Ecuador is considered to be a logistical hub for drug trafficking, where drugs are stockpiled, stored and distributed via Central American routes mainly to the United States, though narcotics are also shipped to Europe.

Police said a woman identified only as María R., with Colombian identity documents, was arrested in Wednesday's operation in the area of Guagua Negro, near the border city of Tulcan, 246 kilometers (153 miles) north of the capital Quito.

The estimated value of the shipment is nearly $842,000 on the domestic market, and more than $11 million in the U.S. and more than $19.6 million (17 million euros) in Europe.

In this image from a video released by Ecuador National Police, Ecuadorian police remove alleged bricks of cocaine from a truck in Carchi, Ecuador, Aug. 12, 2026. Ecuador National Police via AP

In Ecuador, local criminal gangs allied with Colombian and Mexican cartels manage the routes and ship the narcotics, 80% of which originate in Colombia and the rest in Peru.

In the first half of this year, police reported seizing 80 tons of drugs, while in 2025 authorities confiscated nearly 215 tons, primarily cocaine. In 2024, the amount reached almost 295 tons.

Cocaine with creative packaging

Police provided no explanation for the stickers with the image of the golden-haired Norwegian striker. However, it is common practice for drug traffickers to label their shipments with the names of well-known sports figures and other celebrities as a way of signaling which criminal network produced the merchandise and which client it belongs to.

Haaland is not the only soccer star apparently favored by drug smugglers — the image of Argentine national team captain Lionel Messi has also appeared on another seized package.



Packages of drugs are often packaged with other distinct designs. Last year, a beachgoer in Florida found nearly $500,000 worth of cocaine wrapped in "Yosemite Sam" packaging washed up on shore.

A beachgoer found nearly $500,000 worth of cocaine wrapped in "Yosemite Sam" packaging in the Florida Keys, authorities said. Walton County Sheriff's Office

In August 2024, tourists on a Florida beach found a package with 16 bricks of suspected cocaine wrapped in packaging depicting a dune buggy.

In June 2024, boaters off the coast of the Florida Keys found 65 pounds of cocaine — in packages emblazoned with bald eagles —floating in the ocean.

Just weeks earlier, divers found about 55 pounds of cocaine about 100 feet underwater off Key West. Images released by the sheriff's office showed packages marked "Nike SB," with imitations of the footwear brand's iconic swoosh logo on the front.

World.title: Lindsay Clancy sobs loudly, says "I can't do it" amid gruesome trial testimony
World.content:
Lindsay Clancy's murder trial was paused multiple times Wednesday afternoon as she sobbed loudly and said "I can't do it" during testimony about the injuries her children suffered when they were killed.

Jurors were sent out twice for recess as Clancy had emotional reactions to the testimony.

Clancy, 36, is charged with first-degree murder in the deaths of her three children, 5-year-old Cora, 3-year-old Dawson and 8-month-old Callan, in their Duxbury home on Jan. 24, 2023. She has pleaded not guilty.

Prosecutors Jennifer Sprague and Shanan Buckingham said Clancy planned the murders and faked a suicide attempt.

Clancy's attorney Kevin Reddington said Clancy admits to killing her children but says she should not be held criminally responsible because she was overmedicated and suffering from postpartum psychosis.

Defense attorney Kevin Reddington consoles his client, Lindsay Clancy, who is sobbing, during Clancy's murder trial at Plymouth Superior Court in Plymouth, Mass., Wednesday, Aug. 12, 2026. Mark Stockwell/Boston Herald via AP, Pool

Lindsay Clancy sobs during testimony

Dr. Renee Stonebridge from the Office of the Chief Medical Examiner in Boston took the stand Wednesday afternoon. She spoke about the injuries observed on the three Clancy children when the autopsies were performed.

The direct questioning from the prosecution lasted less than 10 minutes, and Reddington did not cross-examine the witness. Clancy could be seen crying during the testimony.

As Sprague began to call the next witness, Judge William Sullivan called for a recess as Clancy was loudly sobbing with her head in her hands. WBZ-TV's Penny Kmitt, who was in the courtroom, said that Clancy's father was crying as well.

After about 15 minutes, all parties came back into the courtroom, including Clancy and the 18 jurors.

Judge Sullivan issued a reminder to the jurors.

"Members of the jury, I just kind of want to revisit an instruction I've given you a few times, I think, during the course of this trial. It's important to understand, remember sometimes as evidence is presented in the trial that creates an emotional reaction, but as jurors who have taken an oath to follow the law, I'm instructing you that the law says you must separate any emotional reaction on your part from the informational value and weight that the evidence produces," Sullivan said. "Your verdict in this case is going to have to be based solely on the evidence and it cannot be based on sympathy, or anger, or passion or prejudice. So you've got to keep that in mind."

Medical Examiner Dr. Barbara Olsen then took the stand. After several minutes, Clancy began to cry again and could be heard on the courtroom microphone saying "I can't do it."

Judge Sullivan sent jurors out of the room. Several minutes later, all parties were back in the courtroom and Olsen was on the stand again.

As Olsen continued to testify, Clancy began sobbing again and laid her head on the table.

Reddington objected at one point, saying, "It's obvious what she wants." He objected several times, becoming visibly frustrated.

Olsen was able to complete her testimony and court ended for the day around 4 p.m. as scheduled.

Witness Latiesha Dukes, a mental health clinician, testifies during Lindsay Clancy's murder trial at Plymouth Superior Court in Plymouth, Mass., Wednesday, Aug. 12, 2026. Mark Stockwell/Boston Herald via AP, Pool

Mental health counselor takes witness stand

Earlier, Latiesha Dukes, a mental health counselor who worked with Clancy, was on the stand for about two hours and stepped down just before 1 p.m.

Dukes, who worked at the time for South Shore Hospital, first met with Clancy in late November 2022 into early December of that year. She met with Clancy four times total during that time period.

Dukes said she worked closest on Clancy's case with Rebecca Jollotta, a psychiatric nurse practitioner who finished her testimony on Tuesday.

"Her presenting concerns were anxiety, lack of sleep, suicidal ideation, thoughts of no longer wanting to live or be here," Dukes said.

Dukes testified that her feeling about Clancy's diagnosis was postpartum anxiety because she did not have anxiety about most things. She recommended outpatient therapy, continued use of medications, and seeing her for weekly therapy.

On Dec. 5, 2022, Clancy reported that she had a difficult weekend and had intrusive thoughts about wanting to die.

Following her meeting with Clancy that day, Dukes said she recommended partial hospitalization.

On Dec. 19, 2022, Dukes said Clancy seemed more engaged during a telehealth visit, was able to smile and laugh and was enjoying time with her family.

Dukes testified that on her last visit with Clancy, she seemed to show an improvement of mood and ability to connect with others. She said that Clancy did not show signs of mania, delusions, paranoia or psychosis.

On cross-examination, Reddington asked about Clancy's reluctance to take medications.

"She was concerned about becoming addicted to medication, yes," Dukes said.

On Tuesday with Jollotta on the stand, Reddington attempted to show that Clancy tried to attend an outpatient postpartum program at Women and Infants Hospital of Rhode Island for two weeks in December 2022, but was turned away on the first day because they wanted to find out if she was overmedicated.

"Would you be surprised if I told you that they said they could not help her because she was overmedicated?" Reddington asked Dukes on Wednesday.

"It would surprise me, yes," Dukes said.

Reddington also questioned Dukes over her testimony that Clancy laughed during her final visit, saying it was not in her notes.

After Dukes stepped down, Cameron Daley, who was working for the Duxbury Police Department and stood watch outside of Clancy's room at Brigham and Women's Hospital after she killed her children, testified for less than five minutes.

Massachusetts State Police investigator testifies

Earlier, Sgt. Dan Lawlor testified. Lawlor has worked for the Massachusetts State Police for nine years.

The night of the children's deaths, Lawlor went to South Shore Hospital in Weymouth and saw Clancy, who was unable to speak and suffering from injuries after jumping out a second-floor window.

Lawlor went to Boston Children's Hospital to check on 8-month-old Callan's status, then later went to Brigham and Women's Hospital, where Clancy was transferred, to stand watch outside the room.

Reddington took over cross-examination after about 15 minutes. The defense attorney asked Lawlor about how no one was allowed to get into Clancy's hospital room. Eventually, Reddington got a court order for psychologist Paul Zeizel to enter the room to meet with Clancy.

"Isn't it fair to say that one of the contentions of the district attorneys is that Paul Zeizel, my doctor, that I got a court order to get in and see her, told her to call Pat and tell him that she heard voices?" Reddington asked.

When Reddington referred to Pat, he was speaking about Patrick Clancy. Lindsay and Patrick Clancy were married at the time of their children's deaths, but have since divorced.

Following that question, the judge asked to see attorneys at sidebar due to an objection by the prosecution. After about 20 minutes, the judge sent jurors out of the room to question Lawlor without the jury present.

With the jury out of the room, Reddington asked about Lawlor's recollection that lead investigator Josh McKelligan had told him that at some point when Clancy was hospitalized, she called Patrick to indicate she was hearing voices. Reddington suggested that the theory investigators were trying to use was that Zeizel had suggested Clancy make the phone call.

"I don't know if it's a theory or not, I just recall the conversation," Lawlor said.

The prosecutor then questioned Lawlor without the jury present.

"You never had a conversation with the prosecution about what the theory was, did you?" she asked. Lawlor said he had not, saying it was only with the fellow trooper.

"Is this conversation guiding your testimony?" Buckingham asked. Lawlor said it was not.

The judge took arguments under advisement and the jury returned a short time later.

With the jury back in the room, Reddington asked Lawlor if he and McKelligan talked about the theory that Zeizel "is the reason that she told her husband she heard voices." Lawlor said they did talk about that theory.

"There's no investigator basis for that, that's McKelligan's speculation, correct?" Reddington asked. Lawlor said that was correct.

Buckingham then questioned Lawlor.

"Is it fair to say you oftentimes will have conversations as investigations are unfolding with other investigators that you're working on the case with about the case, potential evidence, theories of the case?" Buckingham asked.

Lawlor said that was true, and added that theories can change over time.

Buckingham asked Lawlor, "You didn't hear anything that occurred in that room that day that you were there when Dr. Zeizel was there, did you?"

"I did not hear anything," Lawlor said, concluding his testimony at around 10:45 a.m.

Lindsay Clancy listens to testimony during her murder trial at Plymouth Superior Court in Plymouth, Mass., Wednesday, Aug. 12, 2026. Mark Stockwell/Boston Herald via AP, Pool

Lindsay Clancy trial

The jury heard from a psychiatric nurse practitioner Tuesday who specializes in postpartum patients. Rebecca Jollotta said she met with Clancy three times late in 2022, a few weeks before the murders. Jollotta was the 62nd witness in the trial.

Judge William Sullivan said the attorneys told him the proceedings are "well on schedule and somewhat ahead of schedule."

If convicted of first-degree murder, Clancy faces life in prison without parole. If the jury finds that she was not criminally responsible for the deaths of her children, she will be sent to a state psychiatric hospital in Massachusetts.

If you or someone you know is in emotional distress or a suicidal crisis, you can reach the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline by calling or texting 988. You can also chat with the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline here.

For more information about mental health care resources and support, The National Alliance on Mental Illness HelpLine can be reached Monday through Friday, 10 a.m. to 10 p.m. ET, at 1-800-950-NAMI (6264) or email info@nami.org.

"No more operations," he said.

It was mid-January 2026, and my then-73-year-old husband, Mike Salmon, had just started bouncing back from a three-month ordeal of three operations related to aortic aneurysms, sepsis, and a terrifying descent into delirium tied to a stay in the intensive care unit. Now, after another potentially fatal aortic aneurysm and ambulance ride, the doctors clustered around his hospital bed said the fix involved two more major, risky operations.

If Mike did nothing, the aneurysm or sepsis would likely kill him, they predicted. How soon? "Weeks," one doctor said. "I'm astonished I've made it this far," Mike said. So, abruptly, we were shunted onto hospice care — the dead-end spur of the American medical system.

Mike Salmon's health improved so much under hospice care that he got kicked out. Kim Clark for KFF Health News

Hospice agencies manage care for patients expected to die within six months. They don't provide curative procedures or drugs. Instead, they aim to help families make terminally ill patients comfortable, typically at home, as an illness reaches its inevitable conclusion. Families provide most of the day-to-day care, and 85% have suggested they are very satisfied with their hospice's services, which include supplies of drugs and medical equipment, and visits from nurses, therapists, and aides.

More than 1.9 million Americans were enrolled in hospice in the last fiscal year. Over 80% of those patients stayed on hospice until they died — within four weeks, on average. But each year, about 6% of patients are kicked out because a hospice doctor decides they have stabilized or improved enough that they are no longer likely to die in the next six months.

In May, Mike joined that select group. His experience in and out of the hospice system revealed surprising lessons about how families can manage care. And getting removed from hospice revealed a little-known process that can represent a welcome respite for families like ours — but can be devastating for patients with serious chronic illnesses.

Here's what we learned in our four months on and off hospice.

Check before you choose

"Choose one." A hospital nurse handed me a list of local hospice agencies. The sooner we signed up, the sooner Mike could go home. Stunned by the suddenness of Mike's health emergency, I just pointed to the name at the top of the alphabetical list, assuming they were pretty much the same.

Big mistake. Medicare sets basic standards for the hospice agencies it reimburses, but some agencies are understaffed or poorly run. Amy Tucci, president of the Hospice Foundation of America, noted that some agencies provide extra therapy, aide support, and other services.

The problems with the organization I had chosen started immediately. Staffers were often late. They entered inaccurate medical information on Mike's paperwork and didn't make corrections when alerted. Medicare allows you to quit or change agencies, so I asked neighbors for recommendations. That was a good start, but Kristina Newport, chief medical officer of the American Academy of Hospice and Palliative Medicine, said I should also have checked the quality ratings on Medicare's Care Compare site and the National Hospice Locator. Those sites would have alerted me to our first agency's low ratings. Ideally, Newport said, patients or caregivers should call their area's top-rated agencies to find those that provide the services you need, such as staff members who speak the patient's native language, provide spiritual care that aligns with the patient's beliefs, or are stationed nearby to arrive quickly in an emergency.

The local, long-established nonprofit that neighbors recommended handled the transfer seamlessly. Its staff was punctual, accurate, and kind. The chef's kiss after we switched: A nurse from the original company we chose called to say she hoped I hadn't initiated the change because of "concerns about our care of your mother."

Some people get better on hospice

Research hasn't yet fully explored why, but some people actually see their health improve under hospice care. Studies have found, for example, that hospice patients with congestive heart failure or lung cancer live about a month longer, on average, than similar patients in the standard medical system.

Terry Bertholet, who teaches courses on elder law and hospice care at the University of Connecticut, said many patients benefit from hospice's careful pain management, and from leaving hospitals, where they risk infection and overtreatment. Returning home allowed Mike to get up and walk without waiting hours for an overworked nurse to unplug a bunch of monitors, and to enjoy real food. Also, the hospice nurse gave him medicine to help him sleep through the night. He soon started regaining weight and strength.

You can flunk out of hospice for not dying quickly enough

Medicare and many other insurers pay for hospice services only for patients whom physicians certify are likely to die within six months of the most recent assessment (not the date of enrollment), so hospice staff regularly reassess patients. Medicare audits agencies to check for fraud and demands repayment of funds provided for care of patients its auditors deem have not proved to be terminal. Hospices, good and bad, worry about their bottom lines and Medicare's fraud audits. They may feel pressure to discharge patients who threaten the organization's finances, even though such discharges can remove important care. "Medicare is worried about fraud and abuse, not about people not getting enough care," Bertholet said.

Especially for diagnoses with uncertain prognoses — such as dementia — if a patient improves or even stabilizes, hospice physicians might discharge the patient because they can no longer certify a likelihood of death within six months.

For some lucky reason, Mike's aneurysm and sepsis held off. By early May, his wounds had healed, and his strength had improved enough that he returned to gardening, playing bridge, and whipping up his signature lattice-topped blueberry-cinnamon pies. While we appreciated the convenience of the nurse's visits and the drug and medical supply delivery, we realized Mike no longer needed care, so we agreed with our agency's decision to discharge him.

For patients suffering from more debilitating diseases, discharges can be a "nightmare," said Krista Harrison, a hospice researcher at the University of California-San Francisco. Discharges often happen quickly. Medicare requires giving patients a minimum of two days' notice.

When Harrison's father-in-law, suffering from a neurodegenerative disease similar to Parkinson's, was discharged because his health seemed to plateau, the family scrambled to replace and pay for hospice-provided equipment such as a hospital bed and oxygen supply, and they had to quickly find and hire aides to replace the hospice aides. "Just getting his prescriptions reestablished and filled was a big deal," she said. Her father-in-law died six weeks after discharge, she said.

Do your homework to ensure appropriate care

Arming yourself with information about your risks and rights can help you get the hospice care you need when you need it.

Know your diagnosis. Discharges are unlikely for most cancer patients. But patients with dementia, heart disease, and Parkinson's often plateau. So they are disproportionately likely to be discharged, UCSF's Harrison said.

Discharges are unlikely for most cancer patients. But patients with dementia, heart disease, and Parkinson's often plateau. So they are disproportionately likely to be discharged, UCSF's Harrison said. Choose a highly rated hospice. Research shows for-profit hospice agencies are more likely to discharge patients than nonprofits. Medicare's Care Compare site will alert you to which is which.

Research shows for-profit hospice agencies are more likely to discharge patients than nonprofits. Medicare's Care Compare site will alert you to which is which. Keep your own records. Caregivers who can document, say, a patient's growing need for eating assistance can help hospice staff approve continuing care, or build a stronger appeal, UCSF's Harrison said.

Caregivers who can document, say, a patient's growing need for eating assistance can help hospice staff approve continuing care, or build a stronger appeal, UCSF's Harrison said. Keep your family doctor more informed. Doctors "don't have the financial interest" the hospice faces and could help you dispute a discharge, Bertholet advised.

Doctors "don't have the financial interest" the hospice faces and could help you dispute a discharge, Bertholet advised. Appeal quickly. Hospice agencies must provide information on appealing a discharge. But you must file the appeal (online or by phone) by noon on the day before the termination date, which may mean you have only a few hours if you've been given the minimum two days' notice, said Wey-Wey Kwok, a senior attorney for the Center for Medicare Advocacy.

Hospice agencies must provide information on appealing a discharge. But you must file the appeal (online or by phone) by noon on the day before the termination date, which may mean you have only a few hours if you've been given the minimum two days' notice, said Wey-Wey Kwok, a senior attorney for the Center for Medicare Advocacy. Reenroll. Patients can try reenrolling in hospice at any time. Another hospice agency may take you immediately. Or you can wait until the patient's health declines and try reenrolling with your original hospice agency, the Hospice Foundation's Tucci advised.

That last option is our plan. For now, Mike and I are enjoying these unexpected bonus days. But whenever fate catches up with him, Mike said, he's comforted to know he'll get good care from the hospice's staff. "They'll try to improve the quality of what time I have left," he said.

KFF Health News is a national newsroom that produces in-depth journalism about health issues and is one of the core operating programs at KFF — the independent source for health policy research, polling, and journalism.

World.title: Single winning ticket sold for $1.04 billion Powerball jackpot
World.content:
A single ticket in Illinois won a Powerball jackpot of $1.04 billion Wednesday night, the game says. The winning ticket was purchased at a gas station in the city of Quincy, which is on the Mississippi River about halfway down the state.

The winning numbers were 4, 26, 66, 67 and 69, with a Powerball of 9.

The jackpot, which reached the $1 billion mark soon after Monday's drawing didn't produce a winner, was the eighth-largest Powerball grand prize ever and the 15th $1 billion prize in U.S. lottery history.

The cash value for a lump-sum payment was $450.5 million. Winners can also choose to take their prize in 30 payments over 29 years that increase by 5% per year. Both the lump sum payout and the annuity payout totals are before taxes.

Wednesday's jackpot was Powerball's biggest of 2026.

The last time a billion-dollar jackpot was won was last December, when one ticket in Arkansas had all the numbers for a $1.82 billion prize — lotto's second-largest.

Wednesday's drawing was the 44th since a Powerball jackpot was won on May 2, when tickets purchased in Florida and Texas split a $20 million prize.

The drawing was the first to possibly have a winner from the U.K., which began selling tickets in late July. Powerball is played in 45 states, the U.S. Virgin Islands and Washington, D.C. Tickets are $2 each.

The odds of winning a Powerball jackpot are just 1 in 292.2 million.

World.title: Student shot during argument in Georgia high school bathroom, officials say
World.content:
A Warner Robins high school will stay closed for the rest of the week after one student was injured in a shooting Wednesday afternoon on the campus, officials said. A 14-year-old student is in custody.

The Houston County Sheriff's Office reports that the shooting happened at Warner Robins High School. The sheriff's office said that one student was injured in the gunfire and was taken to a local hospital for treatment.

The sheriff's office had initially stated that two people were injured, but Houston County Sheriff Matt Moulton later clarified that only one person was hurt.

An argument in the bathroom of a high school in Warner Robins, Georgia, ended with one student shot and another in custody, officials said. WGXA

In a news briefing Wednesday night, Moulton said the shooting happened at around 2:15 p.m. local time in one of the school's bathrooms. Investigators believe two ninth-grade students got into an argument that eventually escalated, and one of the students pulled out a gun and shot the other, the sheriff told reporters.

The 14-year-old who fired the gun fled the school on foot, Moulton said. The teen was eventually apprehended in a nearby neighborhood.

"Fortunately, what could have been a much worse incident was minimized to us only having one student injured," Moulton said.

Authorities have not said how the teen obtained the firearm, or who it may be registered to. They have also not shared what he may be facing.

Officials say that Warner Robins High School will be closed for the rest of the week for all students. Staff will not come in on Thursday. The school's crisis team will be on campus on Friday and Monday to support students and staff.

Warner Robins is located in Central Georgia, about 100 miles south of Atlanta.

Officials react to shooting at Warner Robins High School

Georgia lawmakers say the Houston County community is in their thoughts after Wednesday's shooting.

Warner Robins Mayor LaRhonda W. Patrick said her community was saddened to hear that the incident could happen so close to home.

"This type of incident impacts our students, faculty, and parents, but also our entire community. We appreciate all of our public safety officers, police and fire, for their rapid response in protection of our children," she wrote on Facebook. "We shall overcome together."

In a statement on X, Gov. Brian Kemp said he was grateful for the men and women who responded to the scene at the high school.

"Their action quickly brought the situation under control and kept students, faculty, and staff safe," Kemp wrote. "As we wait for more details to emerge, we're thankful for all those who keep our classrooms safe."

Sen. Raphael Warnock said he and his office were closely following the reports and that his prayers were with the student who was injured.

"I'm grateful to the law enforcement officers and first responders on the scene," Warnock wrote.
