World.title: Germany: Buildings evacuated over suspected explosive
World.content:
Authorities have begun evacuating buildings around a Bavarian train station as specialists examine a suspicious object on the tracks. Rail traffic is currently suspended in the area.

Buildings near a train station in the southern state of Bavaria were evacuated as a precaution on Thursday after police said that an object found on the tracks could contain explosives.

Investigators later determined that the object was not an explosive, although criminal police were continuing work at the scene.

A technician had discovered the suspicious item in the track bed at the entrance to the station in the town of Treuchtlingen.

Specialists X-rayed the object, which was also lifted using a robot to allow further investigations.

A federal police bomb disposal team is examining the object Image: Felix Kirberg/dpa/picture alliance

Road and rail closures remain in place while the investigation continues. Regional services are affected, with trains terminating early at suitable stations. Replacement buses and large-capacity taxis have been arranged.

Long-distance services are being diverted via the city of Ingolstadt. Police have urged people to avoid the area and take alternative routes.

This is a breaking story that will be updated...

World.title: Germany news: Far-right leader backs left-wing populist
World.content:
08/13/2026 August 13, 2026 Merz calls for defense of democracy on Berlin Wall anniversary

The Berlin Wall started as a barbed-wire barrier but became a massive cement barrier in many places Image: Kindermann/United Archives/IMAGO

Chancellor Friedrich Merz has called on people to keep up the fight to retain freedom and democracy as Germany marks the 65th anniversary of the construction of the Berlin Wall.

"Sixty-five years ago, the leadership of former East Germany had the Wall built. Today, our country has been united longer than it was divided and we live in freedom and peace," Merz wrote on the platform X.

"The lesson of the Wall remains: Freedom and democracy are not a given. We must always fight for them," he wrote.

Merz's remarks come amid a surge in popularity of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD), a party seen by many as anti-democratic in its ideology.

On August 13, 1961, on what would become known as Barbed Wire Sunday, communist East Germany sealed the border between Berlin’s eastern and western sectors before building a wall that was to divide the city for the next 28 years.

People trying to cross the Wall to leave the authoritarian state were often shot dead, and the barrier came to symbolize the repressive political system behind it.

In remarks to the daily Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung, he commissioner for culture, Wolfram Weimer, warned against "positive distortions of former East Germany" by the far-right AfD and the Left Party.

Weimer criticized such "collective forgetting, repression and downplaying of former East Germany" as the biggest challenge to properly commemorating the crimes of the regime there.

World.title: India news: Parliament ends turbulent monsoon session
World.content:
08/13/2026 August 13, 2026 All Air India pilots to undergo mandatory drug testing — report

Air India has ordered a mandatory dope test for all its pilots, starting Thursday, as it expands checks beyond existing regulatory requirements after a pilot involved in a serious mid-air ‌incident ⁠tested ⁠positive for marijuana, reports said citing an internal memo of the country's flag carrier.

The screening would check pilots for any prohibited substances and medications under ​aviation regulations, as per the internal communication.

The tests will be conducted alongside training sessions at ​Air India's academy in Gurugram, or post-flight at the airline's briefing centres and offices, reports said.

Under the existing rules, airlines carry out random testing of at least least 10% of their flight crew for ​psychoactive substances each year..

"We nevertheless now feel that it is important to go further," Reuters cited the internal email from Air India as saying.

The decision comes as Indian aviation authorities probe an incident involving an Air India flight from Phuket to New Delhi on August 4, which suddenly lost about 300 feet (91 meters) of altitude, injuring 20 passengers and four crew members.

The captain of the Airbus A320neo tested positive for marijuana in a confirmatory drug test following the incident.

World.title: Colombia earthquake: Rescue operation enters 'final phase'
World.content:
Rescuers are racing against a critical 72-hour window to find survivors after a magnitude 7.4 earthquake that has killed 265 people, left hundreds missing, and displaced tens of thousands across western Colombia.

Rescuers worked through a third straight night with time ticking towards the 72-hour mark since a powerful earthquake hit Colombia. That's the period aid agencies consider most critical for finding survivors alive, though it can stretch longer if trapped people have access to food and water.

"We're entering the final phase," Cali Mayor Alejandro Eder said, adding that survivors could still be found afterward but that the odds grow steadily worse. He said crews were still detecting signs of life beneath the rubble and urged speed: "Every minute is vital."

Rescue workers ask for silence as they search for survivors at the site of collapsed buildings Image: Raul Arboleda/AFP

The latest on the Colombia earthquake

The death toll from the quake has climbed to 265, President Abelardo de la Espriella said Wednesday.

De la Espriella said roughly 3,500 people have been injured and nearly 500 remain unaccounted for, though a crowdsourced tracking site used by families put the number of missing far higher, at more than 4,100. More than 25,800 families have been affected in total, he said.

The magnitude 7.4 quake — the strongest to hit Colombia in decades — struck on Monday morning near San Jose del Palmar in the northwestern Choco region. It tore through cities across western Colombia, with Cali and Pereira among the hardest hit, along with Manizales and Quibdo.

In Cali, volunteer rescuer Johana Sanchez described teams pausing every 30 minutes to listen for survivors. "So far, three people have been pulled out alive and three dead," she told AFP.

Officials say 140 buildings collapsed entirely and thousands of homes were damaged or destroyed.

Families grapple with human toll

In Palmira, Santiago Lloreda told Reuters the quake killed his mother and his 13-month-old daughter, Salma, who was too young to have fingerprints on file and would need to be identified through DNA testing. He described his mother as the family's caretaker, saying she "gave everything up to look after the baby."

A man who only gave the news agency his first name, Ricardo, traveled from Miami to recover his sister's body and said his niece was awaiting surgery for a fractured skull, jaw and leg, and a collapsed lung: "She's alive. We know she's going to get better."

Colombia races against time after worst quake in a decade To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Thousands have been left homeless, with many sleeping outdoors in parks or emergency shelters set up in schools and sports arenas, either because their homes were destroyed or out of fear of aftershocks.

Colombia's geological service has recorded 130 aftershocks since Monday's quake.

International aid set to pour in

Response efforts have been especially difficult in Choco, the quake's epicenter, a remote and impoverished region already strained by decades of conflict and displacement. Additionally, lost cell service has made it hard to assess damage in communities reachable only by river.

"This earthquake compounds an already severe humanitarian situation, and there is a need for increased support for the humanitarian response," said Giovanni Rizzo, Colombia director for the Norwegian Refugee Council.

And UN resident coordinator María Jose Torres said in a statement Tuesday that aid groups already working in the region on an earlier peace effort were able to pivot quickly to disaster relief.

The United States has pledged more than $15 million and sent response teams. Mexico has sent military aircraft carrying nearly 20 tons of food along with security personnel, with more aid and rescue specialists on standby. El Salvador's president offered two planes carrying 100 tons of supplies, and a search-and-rescue team from Mexico said it arrived directly from Venezuela, which faced its own major earthquakes in June.

Quake response provides test for new Colombian president

De la Espriella, inaugurated just three days before the earthquake struck, declared an economic emergency and three days of national mourning, and pledged to establish a fund to rebuild hospitals, schools, homes and infrastructure.

"This is undoubtedly a tragedy of immense proportions," he said. "Our efforts are focused on those who remain missing." He has not yet detailed what the economic emergency measures will involve.

Notably, de la Espriella won office on a platform of reduced public spending and a tougher security approach. Analyst Tiziano Breda, of the conflict-monitoring group ACLED, told Reuters that de la Espriella had campaigned in part on cutting funding to the country's disaster-response agency — the same unit now leading the emergency effort.

Experts have cautioned that more seismic activity is possible, if not imminent. "Let's remember that Colombia is full of active fault lines," Rodrigo Leon Loya, a seismologist at the University of the Andes, told AP. "The question isn't whether it can happen again. The question is rather when an earthquake of similar magnitude will occur at another of Colombia’s seismic sources," he warned.

Edited by: Rob Turner

World.title: US: Karoline Leavitt to step down as Trump's spokesperson
World.content:
White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt is to leave her job at the end of the month, President Donald Trump says. Leavitt, 28, is the youngest-ever person to have held the position.

Karoline Leavitt, will leave her role as White House press secretary at the end of the month, US President Donald Trump said Tuesday.

Leavitt is one of the best-known faces and most ardent defenders of the MAGA movement.

Trump said in a post on his Truth Social platform that Leavitt was stepping down to "spend more time with her beautiful young children and family," adding that it was "a decision I totally understand and respect!"

Leavitt clung close to Trump as his press secretary Image: Brian Snyder/REUTERS

Who is Karoline Leavitt?

Leavitt, now 28, who took on the job in January 2025 aged 27 at the start of Trump's second term in office, has been the youngest-ever White House press secretary.

She recently returned from parental leave after giving birth to her second child, a daughter, in May. She also has a 2-year-old son.

After initially wanting to be a journalist, Leavitt soon entered politics. She joined the White House press office during Trump's first term, working under then-spokeswoman Kayleigh McEnany.

After Trump lost the 2020 presidential election to Joe Biden, Leavitt worked for the office of Congresswoman Elise Stefanik, a highly loyal Republican supporter of Trump.

Leavitt later unsuccessfully ran for a seat in the House of Representatives in 2022.

She also worked as a spokesperson for MAGA Inc., a super PAC supporting Trump, before joining his successful 2024 campaign.

'The honor and adventure of a lifetime' — Leavitt

In a post on X, Leavitt waxed lyrical about her period in the job.

"Serving as the White House Press Secretary over the past year and a half has been the honor and adventure of a lifetime," Leavitt wrote.

"I am incredibly grateful to President Trump for granting me so many extraordinary opportunities, such as working in the West Wing and spending countless hours in the Oval Office, flying around the world and meeting foreign leaders, and traveling across our beautiful country and meeting Americans from all walks of life."

She said her "bittersweet decision to depart the White House" was due to the difficulties of combining motherhood with the demands of the White House position.

Leavitt: A devoted defender of Trump

Leavitt, who Trump says will remain "one of my top outside advisors, and an influential voice within the Republican Party," has been a key figure in promoting the president's ideology and views, sometimes stretching the truth to do so.

Her very first press conference, on January 28, 2025, was notable for her false claim that $50 million (€43.4 million) in US taxpayers' money had been earmarked to buy condoms in the Gaza Strip.

Since then, she has staunchly defended Trump's hard-line policies while deflecting questions such as those concerning the president's ties with the sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

She was also known for denigrating mainstream media outlets in line with Trump's hostile attitude to reporters who gainsay him.

Her devotion has brought her consistent praise from the president, who has now called her "one ‌of the best White House Press Secretaries in the History of the Office."

World.title: Does the clean energy transition need forever chemicals?
World.content:
As nations globally move to ban forever chemicals, should renewable energy technologies be exempt for the sake of saving the climate?

From solar panels to wind turbines, batteries and hydrogen cells, many renewable energy technologies driving the energy transition share a common ingredient: a class of man-made substances known as "forever chemicals."

The group contains 10,000 synthetic chemicals also known as per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), which persist in the environment and can take thousands of years to degrade.

Widely detected in drinking water, exposure to certain levels of PFAS is linked to increased risk of cancer, suppressed immune function, decreased fertility and developmental delays in children.

These health impacts have inspired bans on well-publicized sources of toxic PFAS such as clothing waterproofing sprays, Teflon non-stick cookware, firefighting foam, packaging and cosmetic products.

While recent bans in France, New Zealand and Denmark target specific PFAS used in consumer products, the European Union wants a broader ban.

PFAS are becoming ever-present in drinking water globally Image: ZDF

The thousands of forever chemicals the EU proposes outlawing includes fluoropolymers, which are valued for their resistance to extreme temperatures, corrosion and UV degradation, and are present in numerous green technologies from lithium-ion batteries to solar panels.

In EV batteries, for example, binders created with PTFE fluoropolymers — also found in Teflon products — are used to coat dry electrodes for greater energy efficiency.

The chemicals industry has pushed back against Europe's mooted ban. An alliance of the world's leading chemical companies, the Performance Fluoropolymer Partnership (PFP) says health concerns about "some types of PFAS" are leading to "unwarranted restrictions" on fluoropolymer production and use.

In a statement on its website describing fluoropolymers as "critical in the fight against climate change," the PFP stated that any bans would "hamstring our climate and energy goals by possibly making the transition more expensive or simply impossible."

Are PFAS necessary to fight climate change?

PFP members include the chemicals arm of US multinational conglomerate, 3M — which is being sued more than $2 billion by the Australian government for its firefighting foam that has leached forever chemicals into the environment — and the Chemours Company, which manufacturers Teflon and was established by chemicals powerhouse, DuPont.

The European Environment Agency says these polymers are considered "relatively less problematic" than the building blocks for PFAS known as monomers. This is due to a larger molecular size that "limits their uptake into living cells" and potential toxicity.

PFAS in water: New solutions and recycling in focus To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Yet fluoropolymers still degrade over time, raising "additional environmental and human health concerns," according to the agency. Experts say these polymers will inevitably emit PFAS during their life cycle and enter the environment — and living organisms — through weathering and physical stress over long periods.

"I don't think we're going to solve the climate crisis by getting cancer," said Gretchen Salter of US-based Safer States, which lobbies to safeguard the environment from toxic chemicals. "You can't demonstrate that these chemicals aren't going to do harm."

"Since chemical makers cannot escape the fact that these types of PFAS are harming our health, they are trying to claim that they are necessary for the clean energy transition," Salter said, adding that research shows how PFAS themselves fuel climate harm and toxic pollution.

The petrochemical industry accounts for 30% of global industrial energy demand — which is higher than the iron, steel and cement sectors — and generates 18% of the industrial sector's greenhouse gas emissions. Overall, chemicals used to produce everything from pharmaceuticals to fertilizers, plastics, paints, electronics and cleaning products are responsible for around 6% of global emissions.

Salter said PFAS categorized as fluorogases (F-gases) are also being marketed as "climate-friendly" since they are used for clean tech like heat pumps, and in electric car batteries. But PFAS gases, though largely non-flammable, are "now the largest source of PFAS pollution globally," she said.

PFAS: Mothers fight against forever chemicals To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

This is partly due to their global warming impact, which is potentially thousands of times higher than carbon dioxide. F-gas leaks can happen throughout a heat pump life cycle via worn seals and improper maintenance and end-of-life disposal. F-gases are also present in fridges and air-conditioning units as a synthetic coolant, where they can leak too.

Are there PFAS-free green tech alternatives?

According to UK-based Chem Trust, which advocates for safer alternatives to toxic chemicals, a suite of PFAS-free clean energy technology is already on the market, including for heat pumps that are being rolled out across Europe as part of a transition from gas heating.

Instead of relying on F-gases, propane is just one alternative energy efficient refrigerant for domestic heat pumps, and with the right design has a negligible fire risk, notes a 2025 Chem Trust report.

The group also says several companies are now producing solar cells without fluoropolymers. Equally, polymer paint that protects wind turbine blades and makes them more efficient is available PFAS-free.

"We are seeing more companies in the EU and across the world embrace the challenge of developing PFAS-free green technologies," said Shubhi Sharma, scientific researcher at Chem Trust, in a statement.

Fluoropolymer boosters claim rechargeable lithium-ion batteries underpinning the energy transition work better with PFAS Image: DR/SP/Andia.fr/IMAGO

But plastics and chemical lobby group Plastics Europe released an assessment report of PFAS-free substitutes in May that argued that "in many critical uses" such as transport, electronics and semiconductors, these alternatives are "either not available or simply do not match the necessary criteria to be considered a viable alternative to fluoropolymers."

Salter of Safer States said efforts to exempt so-called critical and low concern PFAS from class-wide bans means "destroying any sort of incentive to switch to safer alternatives."

"As long as the chemicals industry insists that there are no alternatives, there will be no market to develop any," said the campaigner.

Chemours insists its fluoropolymers and F-gases are "made and used with minimal environmental impact," and says it will achieve a 99% PFAS emissions reduction in the manufacture of fluorinated organic compounds by the end of the decade compared to 2018.

Liz Hitchcock, director of the federal policy program at US environment nonprofit, Toxic-Free Future, told DW that the extreme persistence of PFAS in the environment will inevitably lead to human exposure.

"We've heard claims that there are better PFAS, there are safer PFAS, but we haven't seen the proof."

Edited by: Jennifer Collins

World.title: El eclipse conquista el corazón de España
World.content:
Y el astro rey reveló por fin su corona. Lo hizo bajo un gigantesco manto de sombra que cruzó del norte al este de España a velocidad hipersónica, en apenas siete minutos, desde que entró por la costa cantábrica a las 20.26 hasta que salió por las Baleares a las 20.34 para fundirse con la noche en el mar Mediterráneo. El primer eclipse total que recorre el territorio peninsular desde 1905 cumplió con precisión astronómica los pronósticos; pero al mismo tiempo, sobrecogió a un país que lo esperaba y no recordaba nada semejante. A las ocho y media, el país entero se asomó asombrado hacia el mismo horizonte y más de una lágrima se derramó por las mejillas de quienes lo miraban, que luego se convirtió en una cascada, pero de mensajes que caían sin parar en los grupos de WhatsApp. “Yo también lo estoy viendo”, venían a decirse unos españoles a otros, en innumerables fotos y vídeos compartidos en redes.

Nadie que esté vivo había visto en estas tierras peninsulares esa corona solar, un sedoso velo blanco rodeando una estrella que emergió negra de golpe, casi una hora después de que la Luna nueva comenzase a eclipsarla. Una breve y extraña noche pasó durante un minuto escaso sobre al menos parte de 31 provincias españolas, que no volverán a ver algo así hasta el 17 de noviembre de 2180.

Valerio D'Orazio, de Lisboa (Portugal), utiliza una aplicación de su teléfono móvil para averiguar dónde se verá la fase de totalidad durante el eclipse solar total, en una fiesta para observar el eclipse celebrada en Buitrago del Lozoya (España), el 12 de agosto de 2026. Susana Vera (REUTERS) Una multitud de personas espera con gafas protectoras el comienzo del eclipse de Sol en Madrid este miércoles. SERGIO PEREZ (EFE) Ángela, David y su hijo Diego, de 7 años, posan para hacerse un selfi con gafas protectoras para eclipses durante la fiesta organizada para ver el eclipse solar en Buitrago del Lozoya, España, el 12 de agosto de 2026. Susana Vera (REUTERS) Un hombre prueba unas gafas especiales para observar el eclipse, este miércoles en una playa de Valencia. Alberto Saiz (AP/LaPresse) La Luna comienza a ocultar el Sol en Arija (Burgos). Borja Suarez (REUTERS) Un grupo de personas siguiendo el eclipse en San Sebastián de los Reyes. ÁLVARO GARCÍA Cientos de personas esperan el inicio del eclipse solar en la playa de Riazor en Coruña, este miércoles. Lavandeira (EFE) Un grupo de personas sigue el eclipse desde San Sebastián de los Reyes, este miércoles. ÁLVARO GARCÍA Un paracaidista baja durante el eclipse, en la playa Gurugú en Castellón. Carme RIPOLLE Carme Ripolles El eclipse visto desde San Sebastián de los Reyes. Alvaro Garcia Detalle del eclipse, visto desde Arija. Borja Suarez (REUTERS) Borja Suárez (REUTERS) Una mujer sorprendida mientras contempla el eclipse en Mora la Nova, provincia de Tarragona. GIANLUCA BATTISTA Eclipse Solar desde el Castillo de Montjuic de Barcelona. Massimiliano Minocri Personas congregadas en Benavente, (Zamora), presencian el eclipse en su fase de totalidad. Emilio Fraile Eclipse de Sol junto a un toro de Osborne este miércoles en la localidad de Pradorrey (León). Borja Sanchez-Trillo (EFE) Jazz de Ría Rocío Cibes 12/08/26 ROCÍO CIBES Eclipse solar desde peña izquierda en el Puerto de Montenegro , Soria Victor Sainz Una mujer observa el Sol desde el campo de fútbol de la calle Teide, en San Sebastián de los Reyes. Álvaro García Ambiente previo al eclipse, cerca de un acantilado en Cedeira. ROCÍO CIBES Una mujer fotografía este martes el atardecer y el Cañón del Sil desde el Mirador de Matacás, en Castro Caldelas (Ourense), un día antes del eclipse solar. Brais Lorenzo (EFE) El francés Leyssalle Anthony, de 39 años, prepara un telescopio para observar el eclipse solar total desde la playa de Arija (Burgos), este miércoles. Borja Suarez (REUTERS)

La meteorología también cumplió esta vez con su parte en buena parte de la franja de totalidad. Al menos 15 millones de personas ubicadas bajo esa sombra de unos 300 kilómetros de ancho, prácticamente libre de nubes para la ocasión, tuvieron la oportunidad de mirar directamente el espectáculo natural de un eclipse total perfecto, algo que no puede verse desde ningún otro punto del sistema solar. Solo en la Tierra; y, este 12 de agosto, solo en parte de Islandia y de España, los únicos territorios habitados por los que cruzó la banda de totalidad de este eclipse. En declaraciones a los medios desde el Observatorio de Yebes (Guadalajara), punto oficial de seguimiento del eclipse, el presidente de la Comisión Interministerial para el Trío de Eclipses y secretario de Estado de Ciencia, Innovación y Universidades, Juan Cruz Cigudosa, aseguró que esta cita convertiría a España en “el Mundial de la Astronomía”. “Hoy es la final. España está jugando la final. Está liderando la final”, subrayó. Y desde luego España ganó esa final, para desgracia de los islandeses, que no pudieron ver nada: nubarrones y lluvias opacaron el paso del eclipse por el extremo occidental de la isla, donde Björk había organizado una “rave” solar.

La España vaciada, donde las condiciones eran idóneas para observar el fenómeno, esperaba con la mayor expectación este eclipse. Provincias casi siempre alejadas de la atención, como Soria, Palencia, Teruel o León, concentraron las miradas de todo el mundo y fueron anfitrionas de una celebración única en medio de un verano plagado de romerías. Los festivales masivos de música cedieron el protagonismo a fiestas populares en honor a la alineación perfecta del Sol y la Luna, planeadas con mimo en localidades como Castrillo de la Reina (Burgos), donde la charanga comenzó a recorrer sus estrechas calles a las seis de la tarde, anunciando la doble noche que se avecinaba. Este pueblo, que en invierno solo tiene 121 habitantes, fue el campamento base para más de mil personas llegadas de toda España, que guardaron con celo el secreto de esta ubicación privilegiada ante la posibilidad de una afluencia masiva. A Castrillo de la Reina llegó también una delegación de periodistas del periódico estadounidense The New York Times, que pondría en el centro de atención mundial a esta pequeña localidad de la Sierra de la Demanda. Periodistas internacionales y un festival con aficionados llegados de toda España para ajetrear un pequeño pueblo, perfecta ilustración de lo que supuso este fenómeno astronómico en buena parte de los pequeños municipios que se vieron regados con el premio de la lotería cósmica. “Va a ser como un atardecer sin atardecer”, comentan emocionadas unas adolescentes de Castrillo, ataviadas con las gafas eclipseras en la frente como si fueran gafas de sol fashion.

00:51 Reacciones al eclipse solar total en España El eclipse visto desde Riaño (León). Foto: Néstor Rodan | Vídeo: EPV

La idea de verse desbordados con concentraciones multitudinarias, en medio de un verano que está surfeando una ola de calor tras otra, era la gran preocupación en esa España que enseñaba con orgullo observatorios astronómicos privilegiados como el de Javalambre (Teruel) o que sentía reconocida la bella oscuridad de sus cielos en provincias como Guadalajara, donde las noches de verano que muestran miles de estrellas invisibles en las ciudades, y revelan la Vía Láctea, han sido un auténtico semillero de vocaciones para docenas de astrónomos de primera fila internacional. Esa España que tiende un puente científico con Marruecos —en tiempos tan complicados con el vecino del sur— para ensayar en la ciudad de Palencia un experimento científico que se completará el 2 de agosto de 2027, cuando otro eclipse total cruce el extremo sur de la Península y el norte de África.

Si lo normal es que pasen casi 400 años para que un eclipse total vuelva a pasar por el mismo lugar, las regiones que han vivido este miércoles el día de las dos noches pueden considerarse especialmente afortunadas. Otro eclipse con un recorrido muy similar pasó por la mayoría de ellas en 1905, dejando huella en la memoria colectiva. En Castrillo de la Reina, los más viejos del lugar recuerdan cómo sus mayores les hablaron de aquella vez que la gran sombra de la Luna les cogió por sorpresa, hace 121 años y también a mediados del siglo XIX. Aunque el país entero llevase meses hablando del fenómeno astronómico, cuyo paso la ciencia había predicho al segundo, cuando de verdad llegó dejó una mezcla de júbilo y estupor que nos hizo empatizar con nuestros antepasados que vivían con miedo esa súbita oscuridad, que siempre llegaba por sorpresa.

La eclipsemanía pasó por España por primera vez desde que toda la población tiene acceso libre a la información sobre los detalles de la ocultación total del Sol —y a los medios de protección adecuados para observar el fenómeno sin riesgos para la vista—, resucitó preocupaciones que conectan con algunos de esos miedos ancestrales. Colegios de oftalmólogos y departamentos ministeriales recomendaron a la población que observase el eclipse total con las gafas de protección puestas todo el tiempo, ante el temor a graves lesiones oculares por su uso incorrecto. Mientras tanto, pequeños pueblos como Frómista (Palencia) prefirieron organizar observaciones públicas con maestros de ceremonias como el astrofotógrafo Ángel de Francisco, que dio precisas indicaciones a sus vecinos sobre cuándo tenían que quitarse las gafas para poder observar, sin riesgos, lo que siempre está ahí pero nunca habíamos podido ver: la corona solar.

Un reto para el país

Justo cuando la Luna comenzaba a morder la luz del Sol, el ministro del Interior, Fernando Grande-Marlaska, informaba en Yebes de que el comienzo del operativo —que había anunciado el despliegue de casi 35.000 efectivos, entre policías y guardias civiles— se había desarrollado sin demasiados incidentes. A primera hora de la tarde, algunos atascos a la salida de Madrid y Barcelona, que no se habían llevado el premio gordo del eclipse total, mostraban las ganas de la ciudadanía de llegar a un evento único. Atascos que se repitieron entrada la noche, de regreso. Y también en la costa asturiana, castigada por las nubes.

El Gobierno instaló su cuartel general en el Observatorio Astronómico de Yebes, levantado en 1975 en este pueblo de Guadalajara de más de 5.600 habitantes por sus casi 1.000 metros de altitud, pero a pesar de los rumores, desmentidos desde La Moncloa, no apareció por allí Pedro Sánchez, que solo disfrutó de un eclipse parcial en la residencia de La Mareta, en la isla canaria de Lanzarote. Aunque la totalidad del 100% oculto solo ensombreció al 40% del territorio español, todo el país, hasta el archipiélago canario, disfrutó de su trocito de eclipse.

01:43 Seis lugares distintos que han visto el eclipse Varias personas observan el eclipse en Arcos de Salinas (Teruel), este miércoles. Foto: Christian Hartmann (REUTERS) | Vídeo: EPV

El Gobierno preveía entre 400.000 y 1,5 millones de desplazamientos adicionales para acudir a zonas donde el fenómeno se observara en su totalidad, por lo que se había desplegado un dispositivo especial de vigilancia de la Dirección General de Tráfico. También se temía una caída de las comunicaciones por saturación y, sobre todo, había temor por el riesgo de incendios, como señaló la ministra para la Transición Ecológica y el Reto Demográfico, Sara Aagesen: “Prohibido encender fuego, no aparcar sobre vegetación seca, mantener los accesos libres para emergencias y consultar diariamente el nivel de peligro de incendios. El día del eclipse solar total es un día para disfrutar, pero también una llamada a la prudencia y a la precaución”.

El cálculo de los beneficios para las provincias agraciadas por la lotería astronómica estimaba medio millón de turistas extra gracias al astroturismo y entre 350 y 400 millones de euros de valor añadido. Pero la ciencia tomó la palabra para reivindicarse en tiempos oscuros, y no por la sombra del eclipse. El astronauta, exministro de Ciencia y presidente de Hispasat, Pedro Duque, expresó su deseo de que el eclipse “atraiga a la gente hacia el conocimiento” y de que “quede en la conciencia” de los españoles. En declaraciones a los medios en el Observatorio del Ebro, en Roquetes (Tarragona), insistió en luchar contra la desinformación con el poder de la ciencia: “Hay gente que hace más caso a un audio de WhatsApp que te viene de la vecina del quinto que a las cosas que realmente funcionan, como la ciencia”.

En ese mismo sentido, su sucesora, Diana Morant, defendió en RNE que “es imposible una conversación entre ciencia y un charlatán”. “La humanidad siempre ha mirado al cielo para explicar las cosas y cuando no existía la ciencia se pensaba que eran los dioses los que castigaban”, dijo la ministra. “Se buscaban explicaciones y ahora las explicaciones las tenemos en la ciencia y no hay una ciencia que explique el cambio climático y una ciencia que diga que no hay cambio climático”, insistió. Más allá de la confrontación política, una cita científica, un eclipse total histórico, llenó de asombro a media España, hipnotizada por la belleza de la imagen que grabó en sus retinas.

World.title: El turismo, la fábrica de oportunidades de España
World.content:
Con cerca de 700.000 empresas y un récord de visitantes en el horizonte, el sector de los viajes, el alojamiento y el ocio premia a los emprendedores que se especializan en un nicho del mercado, buscan soluciones digitales o convierten la sostenibilidad en una ventaja competitiva

Si hay una industria proclive al emprendimiento ahora mismo en España, esa es la del turismo. Este boyante sector, uno de los principales motores económicos nacionales, no para de batir sus propias cifras. Este año se prevé que se acerque a los 100 millones de visitantes —después de alcanzar los 96,8 millones en 2025—, algo nunca visto en el segundo país más visitado del mundo, solo por detrás de Francia. Y ese volumen inédito, explica David Hernández, fundador de la agencia de viajes personalizados Pangea, genera oportunidades de negocio en toda la cadena de valor: desde los alojamientos a la restauración, el ocio y el transporte.

Triunfar en el sector, asegura Asier Baquero, director del máster en Innovación en Turismo de la Universidad Internacional de La Rioja (UNIR), requiere, no obstante, de estrategia. “Hoy no basta con montar un hotel y esperar a que lleguen los huéspedes; el crecimiento también ha multiplicado la competitividad, por lo que resulta esencial diferenciarse para destacar”, explica el experto. Algo que se consigue a través de la adopción de soluciones innovadoras, de la especialización o de la atención a la creciente sensibilidad de los visitantes por la sostenibilidad.

Consejo de empresario Para emprender hay que ser optimista, pero si te pasas de la raya, te puedes llevar sorpresas David Hernández, Fundador de la agencia de viajes personalizados Pangea

Digitalización para abrirse camino en el mercado

Las soluciones digitales se han convertido en una palanca de diferenciación en el sector del turismo. Hoy la mayoría de las empresas de éxito nacen en el ecosistema de start-ups para ofrecer soluciones directamente al consumidor. Es el caso de la barcelonesa ByHours, que comercializa habitaciones por horas en hoteles de todo el mundo, o el de la madrileña Civitatis, que ha revolucionado el mercado de las actividades turísticas en español al programar visitas guiadas y excursiones por ciudades de Europa, Latinoamérica, Estados Unidos y Asia. “Ambas han identificado una necesidad del turista y han aportado una solución digital que, además, se puede exportar a cualquier parte del globo”, puntualiza Baquero, que da una pista de por dónde puede ir el emprendimiento: “El objetivo de España ya no es atraer más a turistas, sino gestionar de manera más eficiente la estancia de los que visitan el país”.

Otras empresas de ese ecosistema digital, explica Baquero, se crean con el objetivo de brindar soluciones a las grandes agencias de viajes o a las cadenas hoteleras. “Así sucede con los asistentes de inteligencia artificial para centralitas que gestionan las llamadas de los hoteles y las conectan con las reservas, algo que les permite ahorrar muchos recursos”, explica Baquero.

Jugar la baza de la especialización y la sostenibilidad

Encontrar una solución para un grupo concreto de consumidores es otra de las maneras de empezar con buen pie en el sector. Baquero afirma que hoy los hoteles o las agencias de viaje necesitan un apellido: “Un hotel burbuja, una agencia de viajes de lujo o para el segmento LGTBIQ+...”, ejemplifica el experto. Esta es una de las razones que explica el éxito de Nomading Camp, una empresa especializada en alojamientos de lujo en entornos naturales, con propuestas como suites y habitaciones burbuja en cinco destinos, desde los Pirineos hasta la sierra malagueña de Ronda. Lo justifica su fundador, Miquel Vila: “En nuestro caso, la experiencia es muy importante. No ofrecemos solo una cama, sino una noche en pleno bosque con todas las comodidades. La propia habitación es la experiencia. Nuestros clientes no nos escogen porque quieren ir a un destino y necesitan un sitio para dormir, sino que primero escogen nuestra experiencia y luego se desplazan hasta donde van a vivirla”, describe el empresario.

Emprender en el turismo tiene una dificultad añadida frente a otros sectores: no se venden productos, sino experiencias. Un fabricante puede controlar casi todas las características de lo que produce, pero una empresa turística depende de multitud de factores que determinan cómo recordará el cliente su viaje: la atención, el clima, las expectativas del viajero, la coordinación entre distintos servicios... Por eso, el éxito no consiste solo en ofrecer un buen servicio, sino en conseguir que el visitante viva una experiencia que merezca la pena recomendar, defiende Hernández, de Pangea. “Vendemos viajes a destinos cercanos, pero también a 10.000 kilómetros de distancia, con 20 proveedores, por lo que hay una alta probabilidad de que algo salga mal”, destaca.

Consejo de empresario Sigue tu propio camino sin fijarte en el camino de otros emprendedores Miquel Vila, fundador de los alojamientos de lujo en plena naturaleza Nomading Camp

La sostenibilidad gana cada vez más peso como ventaja en esta industria, asegura Baquero. Porque no solo responde a una creciente demanda de los viajeros, sino que también contribuye a reducir costes, acceder a financiación y cumplir la normativa. Por eso cada vez más compañías deciden que su propuesta de valor esté claramente ligada a la sostenibilidad, la economía circular o la conservación del entorno. La catalana Turismo Vivencial se ha hecho un hueco en el mercado ofreciendo consultoría sobre ecoturismo, el turismo respetuoso con el medio ambiente, y organiza actividades que contribuyen a conservar el patrimonio natural y cultural, así como generar beneficios a las comunidades locales. Cada vez son más comunes las compañías que ayudan a negocios del sector a medir su impacto ambiental, como la valenciana Bioscore Sustainability y la madrileña GreeMKO, que no es exclusiva del sector turístico, pero desarrolla programas para la gestión ambiental y el cálculo automatizado de la huella de carbono de hoteles.

Lecciones de los emprendedores

David Hernández y Miquel Vila, que protagonizan el último capítulo de El poder de las empresas, el pódcast de los que hacen , de Banco Sabadell, comparten algunas de las lecciones que han aprendido después de emprender y que pueden ser de utilidad para los empresarios de hoy y mañana. Vila, de Nomading Camp, asegura que, con el tiempo y la distancia, le hubiera gustado compararse menos con otros emprendedores y haber hecho caso a su instinto más frecuentemente: “Merece la pena seguir tu propio camino. Por ejemplo, si tus competidores están haciendo rondas de inversión y tú sientes que no necesitas una nueva, no la hagas; tu gran meta ha de ser que tu negocio funcione, no la ronda en sí misma”. Hernández, de Pangea, señala una actitud como clave a la hora de enfrentarse a cualquier decisión: “No hay que ser demasiado optimista. Me explico: creo que para ser emprendedor es imprescindible ser optimista, pero si te pasas de la raya luego te puedes llevar sorpresas”.

World.title: 16 pueblos españoles que piden manga larga cuando cae la tarde
World.content:
Vielha (Lleida). La gran baza de los pueblos seleccionados radica, sobre todo, en la posibilidad de tener que taparse para descansar, algo que se ha convertido en todo un lujo durante la canícula. Es un requisito que cumple Vielha, a la vera de los ríos Garona y Nere, con su casco histórico construido a la manera aranesa, a golpe de piedra, pizarra y madera. Sus mínimas descenderán hasta los 12ºC la noche del domingo; las máximas alcanzarán picos de 33ºC en las horas centrales del jueves y viernes, pero bajarán a los 24ºC (y con probabilidad de lluvias) el lunes, según la Aemet. La capital del Valle de Arán se presenta como un buen campamento base para conocer este territorio del Pirineo catalán, con sus 33 núcleos de población, sus algo más de 10.000 habitantes y sus iglesias románicas. Es recomendable acercarse a la cascada Saut deth Pish, probablemente la más bonita de la zona. Más información: visitvaldaran.com/descubre-la-val-daran/pueblos/vielha/.

World.content:

One person has been killed and several others injured in an explosion at a site in the Port of Rotterdam, police say.

The blast happened shortly after midday on Thursday at a company on the Moezelweg in Europoort, regional broadcaster Rijnmond reported. Police said they had no further information at this stage.

Multiple people were injured and taken to hospital. Six ambulances, a trauma helicopter and fire crews were sent to the scene.

Rijnmond reported that a hired maintenance crew had been working on pipelines at the site and that something may have gone wrong as those pipes were being disconnected.

Traces of an explosion were visible on a storage tank, the broadcaster said.

Earlier on Thursday, a power cut shut down systems at the Esso refinery on the Botlekweg, sending large flames and black smoke over the port as gas lines were emptied. The Rotterdam-Rijnmond safety authority said it had not established whether the incidents were connected.

World.title: Amsterdam researchers find remedy for fatal child brain disease
World.content:
Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Researchers from the Emma Children’s Hospital at Amsterdam UMC have for the first time found a way to treat a rare genetic brain disease found mostly in children – vanishing white matter, or VWM.

According to The Lancet Neurology, which published the findings, VWM is a neurodegenerative disease “with onset mostly in children aged 1–6 years that causes early death and has no effective therapy.” It’s caused by a genetic defect and occurs in 1 in 100,000 people in the Netherlands.

But now the blood pressure drug guanabenz has been found to inhibit the disease.

In a trial at Amsterdam UMC, 33 children from various countries received guanabenz for four years, while the comparison group included 66 children who did not receive it. Children who received the drug stabilised and ended up needing a wheelchair less often and less quickly.

They also lived – as compared to five patients in the comparison group who died.

“We saw that the disappearance of the white matter in the brain slowed down or even stopped,” chief researcher Marjo van der Knaap told broadcaster NOS.

Moving forward, “the disease-modifying effect of guanabenz should be confirmed in a long-term extension study,” wrote the researchers. The drug also needs the approval of the European Medicines Agency to be used as a treatment for VWM.

World.title: Once-in-a-lifetime solar eclipse has Netherlanders over the moon
World.content:
Eclipse mania took over the Netherlands Wednesday night as people flocked to the coast, roofs and open spaces to watch the largest solar eclipse of the past few decades.

“It looks like a moon giving off light,” a woman on the beach in Petten, a village about 60 kilometers northwest of Amsterdam on the North Sea, told broadcaster NOS. “This is truly very special.”

Indeed traffic jams were rampant on the roads to the sea. But weather conditions were perfect for viewing the eclipse, which was broadcast live on NOS. Some of its broadcasters were clearly moved by the phenomenon.

“This is making me a bit emotional,” NOS weatherman Peter Kuipers Munneke said.

Underwhelmed

But others were less enthusiastic.

College student Sophie joined the crowds to watch the eclipse from the Marineterrein in Amsterdam Oost. Originally planning to make glasses out of old photo negatives, her friend managed to get hold of the hard to come by eye protectors in Amstelveen. But after all the effort, she said they were underwhelmed.

“It wasn’t that special,” she told Dutch News. “The moon didn’t even cover the sun fully. It was like 88% covered and all the sudden, everyone clapped and the sun came back. It wasn’t a total eclipse like in Spain, and it didn’t really become dark. But we had fun.”

A solar eclipse occurs when the moon passes between the sun and earth, blocking all or some of the sun’s light and casting a shadow over the earth.

World.title: Drought means less honey this summer as nectar dries up
World.content:
The persistent drought in the Netherlands has now affected beekeepers, who have noticed that honey production is down this summer. Flowers are blooming for a shorter period, if at all, making it impossible for honeybees to collect the nectar they need to survive.

Professional beekeeper and secretary of the Professional Beekeepers’ Association John Hoogendoorn chalks it up to climate change. “There are increasingly longer periods of drought and higher temperatures, which changes the habitat of the bees,” he told broadcaster NOS. “Nature and the rich biodiversity have deteriorated over the years.”

He said the damage is particularly acute on the dry sandy soils in the east of the country, where the heather honey season has only just begun. Beekeepers report seeing dry shrubs and very little purple, flowering heather there.

Beekeeper Frauke Wessel from Haarlemmermeer has also seen the change. “The bees bring in food to keep their colony alive. But we notice that the honeycomb is no longer filled. The queen bee also lays fewer eggs because she does not get enough food,” she told NOS.

Honeybees need nectar to give them energy for flight and other daily colony tasks. They also convert any excess nectar into stored honey to get them through flowerless winters.

Because the honeybees can’t build up their winter supplies this rainless summer, beekeepers like Hoogendoorn are making up for the lack of honey with dissolved sugar. He told NOS that he needs about 15 kilos of sugar per colony this year to substitute for the honey shortage. “That’s more than in previous years.”

Bees are usually active in the country from the end of February until mid-September. “But due to the high temperatures, the bee season lasts longer and starts earlier,” said beekeeper Joris Knoops.

Flies, wasps, mosquitoes and dragonflies are also suffering from the lack of water.

World.title: Your takeaway habit is feeding Dutch inflation, says DNB
World.content:
Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Dutch households are spending so much on takeaway meals that it is impacting national inflation, the Dutch central bank DNB has reported.

Delivery meals have nearly doubled as a share of the average shopping basket, from around 1.6% in 2015 to just over 3% today, DNB said on Thursday.

Prices have climbed fast. With more people spending, delivery firms have also passed on higher wage, energy and ingredient costs, and between 2020 and 2023 the category went from adding less than 0.1 percentage point to inflation to a full 0.35 point.

It has since eased back to 0.13 point – but only because prices stopped rising so fast, not because anyone is ordering less, DNB said.

The bank traces consumer habits back to the Covid pandemic, when locked-down households began using ordering apps much more, especially while working from home.

Dutch inflation has sat above the European Central Bank’s 2% target for years, driven mainly by rents and food prices. The pizza and sushi deliveries are now also hitting the figures.

World.title: Monument against violence in youth care system vandalized
World.content:
Just two months after it was unveiled, the national youth care monument (Nationaal Monument Jeugdzorg) commemorating violence against young people in the system was vandalised in Apeldoorn.

“This feels like a new attack,” Naomi van Aggelen told broadcaster NOS. She worked for years on the monument and was herself wrongly sent to live at a youth care institution when she was 12 years old.

“It is a very sad sight,” she said of the monument meant to acknowledge the suffering of young people in care homes. “Actually, [it’s] a denial of that recognition.”

Located in Apeldoorn’s Zuiderpark, the wings of the monument – titled De Erkenning (The Recognition) – were broken off and are now missing while scratches and dents are visible on what remains.

“Who does such a thing? We have no idea,” said Van Aggelen. “We don’t know where the wings are.”

The council has filed a police report and is said to be reviewing if additional security measures are needed.

The monument was commissioned after a 2019 report by De Winter Commission that found since WW2, some 20,000 children were the victims of violence in youth care. The organising foundation calls it a place of reparation, remembrance and “of vigilance: all current forms of violence must also stop.”

The future of the monument is still unclear. “I have no idea if we should leave the work for what it is,” said Van Aggelen. “Maybe we should glue it, then it symbolises another broken child in youth care.”

World.title: Barcelona legend Xavi appointed Netherlands head coach
World.content:
Xavi Hernández has been appointed head coach of the Netherlands men’s national team on a contract running to the 2030 World Cup, the Dutch football association KNVB has announced.

The 46-year-old Spaniard succeeds Ronald Koeman, who stepped down after the Netherlands’ last-32 defeat by Morocco at this summer’s World Cup. His appointment ends a long and closely watched search, and comes as a surprise after several higher-profile names fell away.

Former Feyenoord and Liverpool coach Arne Slot, ex-Ajax and Manchester United manager Erik ten Hag and PSV’s Peter Bosz all ruled themselves out, while the KNVB passed over Jong Oranje coach Michael Reiziger and Louis van Gaal. On

Tuesday, Roberto Martínez was reportedly the front-runner, though the KNVB never held direct talks with him.

“A son of Dutch football”

Xavi becomes the first foreign coach of Oranje since the Austrian Ernst Happel, who led the side to the 1978 World Cup final.

“It is a great honour to become head coach of the Netherlands national team,” he said in a statement released by the KNVB. “As someone who was developed at the FC Barcelona academy, with strong influences from, among others, Johan Cruyff and Rinus Michels, I feel a special connection to Dutch football. You could say I am, in a way, a son of Dutch football.”

As a player, Xavi is regarded as one of the best midfielders of his generation, winning four Champions League titles in more than 750 games for Barcelona and lifting the 2010 World Cup with Spain – beating the Netherlands in the final – as well as the European Championship in 2008 and 2012.

He started out as a coach at Al Sadd in Qatar, then took charge of Barcelona in 2021 – also succeeding Koeman – and won the Spanish league title in 2023, but made little impression in Europe before leaving in 2024.

Restoring tactics

The KNVB has handed Xavi an explicit task: restore the attacking, possession-based football long associated with the Dutch game, after a World Cup exit widely seen as a low point in style as much as result.

“As a coach, he has been shaped by years of working with top coaches who share a footballing vision that aligns very well with the way we want the Netherlands national team to play,” said the KNVB’s director Nigel de Jong. He pointed to “taking the initiative, playing dominant and attractive football, combined with the flexibility required in modern football at the highest level.”

Xavi said he shared that ambition. “The Netherlands has a rich football culture and a clear vision that strongly appeals to me: attacking football, based on possession, with creativity, passion and conviction,” he said. “The main objective is always to win, but I prefer to do so in a way that reflects those characteristics and that people can enjoy watching.”

He will be presented at the KNVB’s Zeist headquarters on August 25 and takes charge for the first time on September 24, at home to Germany in the Nations League.

World.title: NL breaks 1947 heat record with 31 tropical days in a year
World.content:
The Netherlands has recorded more tropical days in a single year than at any point since records began, after the temperature hit 31.5° in Maastricht on Tuesday.

It was the 31st day this year on which 30° or more – the threshold for a tropical day – was reached somewhere in the country, beating the record of 30 set in 1947.

Back then, the 30th tropical day did not arrive until September. This year the record fell in mid-August with weeks of potential summer heat still to come, and forecasters expect the tally to rise further.

The national weather service KNMI has linked the growing number of tropical days and back-to-back heatwaves to climate change.

The heat coincides with the second driest summer since measurements began in 1901 – only 1976 was drier – with the Rhine at its lowest in almost 80 years.

The public health institute RIVM has reactivated its national heat plan for the fourth time across the whole country from Wednesday, urging people to check on the elderly and young children and to keep homes cool.

Friday is forecast to be the hottest day, with highs of 33° to 37° and the chance of a fifth regional heatwave of the year, before cooler air moves in at the weekend.

The personal data of almost 19 million people, including medical information, has been compromised in a major cyberattack on a company that provides services to thousands of medical facilities in Poland. “We are dealing with one of the largest incidents in Poland’s history,” said digital affairs minister Krzysztof Gawkowski on Wednesday. He urged people to use government services to check whether their data is affected and to “lock” their national identity number to prevent potential fraud. W związku z sytuacją krytyczną zostały natychmiast podjęte działania mające zabezpieczyć dane i wyjaśnić okoliczności incydentu –… pic.twitter.com/nIp6EvbKiu — Ministerstwo Cyfryzacji (@CYFRA_GOV_PL) August 12, 2026 The attack targeted MyDr, a company that provides services used by many medical facilities in Poland. Its data includes patients’ personal information, as well as medical details such as diagnoses and prescriptions. It was first reported on Monday by Zaufana Trzecia Strona, an IT security news service, which said that it had been contacted on Saturday by the alleged perpetrators, who claimed to have accessed the data of around 18.8 million people. The hackers, who have not been identified, had also sent a screenshot from the compromised database showing the personal data of “one of the most important politicians in Poland”, added Zaufana Trzecia Strona. Shortly afterwards, MyDr confirmed that it had “become the target of an external, deliberate criminal activity involving some of our data”. In an update on Wednesday, it said that, at the time of writing, there was no evidence that the data had been published anywhere. Największy wyciek danych osobowych w historii Polski i co możemy z nim zrobić – nasza analiza incydentu w MyDr i jego potencjalnych skutków.https://t.co/vXUmVfpPAP Opisujemy aktualny stan wiedzy i możliwe scenariusze rozwoju sytuacji. pic.twitter.com/uqhjz1CjZ1 — ZaufanaTrzeciaStrona @zaufanatrzeciastrona@infosec (@Zaufana3Strona) August 13, 2026 Gawkowski addressed the issue at a press briefing on Wednesday. He noted that “there is no indication we are dealing with an external attack…from Russia or any other country”. Poland has recently regularly been targetted by Russian state-linked hackers. It is “very likely” that cybercriminals are behind the attack on MrDr, said Gawkowski, who pledged that there would be an “uncompromising” response from the Polish security services. The minister advised Poles to check in a secure government database whether their data had been leaked. He also advised citizens to use the state web portal, known as mObywatel, to “lock” their identity number, known as a PESEL, which prevents fraudsters from using it. Around 12,000 medical facilities use MyDr’s services, the digital affairs ministry told the Polish Press Agency (PAP). The company claims that it processes three million medical consultations and 2.7 million prescriptions a month, reports the Gazeta Wyborcza daily. World.title: Fugitive Polish opposition politician reportedly in pro-Russian Moldovan breakaway region
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! A letter sent to a Polish court by Marcin Romanowski, who served as a deputy justice minister in the former national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government and is now on the run from criminal charges, suggests that he is residing in Transnistria, a breakaway region of Moldova that has close links with Russia. The Polish authorities have been trying to locate and extradite Romanowski, whose whereabouts have been unknown since he fled Budapest earlier this year after Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán, who had granted him asylum, lost power. Były wiceminister sprawiedliwości ma przebywać w Tyraspolu, stolicy zbuntowanej mołdawskiej prowincji znajdującej się pod patronatem Rosji. Spod tego adresu w Naddniestrzu polityk PiS miał wystąpić o wydanie listu żelaznego.https://t.co/m05dtQv3KV — Rzeczpospolita (@rzeczpospolita) August 12, 2026 On Wednesday, following media reports that Romanowski had sent a letter to the Polish authorities from Transnistria, a spokeswoman for Warsaw’s district court, which is responsible for extradition matters, confirmed to news website Gazeta.pl that this was the case. “The letter and envelope indicate that the package was sent to the court from Tiraspol in Transnistria,” said judge Anna Ptaszek. “It bears his handwritten signature.” Przemysław Nowak, the spokesman for Poland’s National Prosecutor’s Office, also confirmed to broadcaster RMF that Romanowski had sent the letter, in which he indicated that he was residing in Tiraspol, the capital of Transnistria, and requested safe passage to Poland. The fugitive politician said that he would be willing to appear in court or before prosecutors, on the condition that he was not placed in detention, said Nowak, who added that prosecutors had not yet taken a position on Romanowski’s request. Transnistria is a region of eastern Moldova, bordering Ukraine, that sought to become a separate state in the early 1990s, even fighting a war between 1990 and 1992. Today, the territory, which has a population of around 360,000, operates as a de facto state but is not recognised by any other country. Transnistria has close ties with Russia, which maintains a military “peacekeeping” force there. The territory’s flag and national emblem feature the Soviet hammer and sickle. Romanowski’s apparent presence in the Russian-linked territory was condemned by figures from Poland’s government. “I would say that Romanowski is now very likely under the influence of Russian intelligence,” said deputy defence minister Cezary Tomczyk, quoted by broadcaster TVN. Paweł Wojtunik, the former head of Poland’s Central Anticorruption Bureau (CBA), who previously worked in Moldova, wrote that “it is impossible to enter [Transnistria], let alone to live there, without the consent of the local KGB, which is directly managed by the Russian GRU and FSB [intelligence agences]”. – Dzisiaj powiedziałbym, że Romanowski z dużym prawdopodobieństwem jest pod wpływem rosyjskich służb – ocenił wiceszef MON Cezary Tomczyk. Sprawę skomentował też szef MSZ Radosław Sikorski.https://t.co/LuWw0bkh2j — tvn24 (@tvn24) August 12, 2026 Even a deputy leader of Romanowski’s own party, the national-conservative PiS, was unwilling to defend him. In an interview with Polsat News, Przemysław Czarnek noted that it is still not confirmed that Romanowski is in Transnistria. But he agreed, when asked by the host, that it “would be crossing a line” for Romanowski to be in the territory. Romanowski served as a deputy justice minister in the former PiS government between 2019 and 2023. He remains a member of parliament, despite having fled Poland in December 2024 after prosecutors sought to bring charges against him for 11 alleged crimes, including participating in an organised criminal group. Those alleged offences relate to Romanowski’s time at the justice ministry, which was then led by Zbigniew Ziobro, who is also wanted on multiple charges. Both Romanowski and Ziobro obtained asylum in Hungary when the country was led by PiS-ally Orbán. The Polish government says that Hungary has revoked the refugee status and travel documents granted to fugitive ex-justice minister Zbigniew Ziobro by Viktor Orbán. Poland will now seek Ziobro's deportation from the US, where he fled after leaving Hungary https://t.co/TcVw0AiEMX — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 2, 2026 However, after Orbán lost power earlier this year, Ziobro fled to the United States, where he remains. Last month, Poland requested his extradition, though that is a process that could take years. Romanowski, meanwhile, disappeared completely, leading to months of speculation as to his whereabouts. Both politicians have denied the allegations against them and have claimed to be victims of “political revenge” by the current government, a more liberal coalition led by Prime Minister Donald Tusk that took power in December 2023. They have argued that they would not be able to receive a fair trial in Poland while Tusk remains in power because of the government’s influence over the judicial system. On Wednesday, Romanowski’s lawyer, Bartosz Lewandowski, confirmed that his client had requested safe passage to Poland and that he was “outside the territory of the European Union”. However, he did not confirm that Romanowski is in Transnistria. Poland has formally asked the US to detain and extradite former justice minister @ZiobroPL, who faces multiple criminal charges. World.title: Poland complains to Starlink over exclusion from European roaming zone

The Polish government has appealed to Starlink, the satellite internet service operated by Elon Musk’s SpaceX, to reverse its decision to exclude Poland from its European roaming area. It says that Polish users, who will now face greater costs when travelling, should not be treated as “second-tier customers”. Starlink, which provides users with portable terminals that act as receivers for internet connections from its network of satellites, offers a “Roam” service that lets customers continue using their connection outside their home country without extra charges as long as they remain within their designated region. One region is Europe, in which Starlink has included 36 countries and territories. However, the firm makes clear that “Poland is not included in the Europe region”, meaning users registered in that country are not included in the Roam system. The company offered no explanation for Poland’s exclusion from the system. Some media reports have suggested that it is because terminals registered in Poland are used in Ukraine. However, Ukraine is itself not included in Starlink’s European “Roam” region. The company’s decision prompted an angry response from Polish government ministers. “I do not agree with a global technology company treating Poles worse than other Europeans,” wrote digital affairs minister Krzysztof Gawkowski on X, the social media platform owned by Musk. “If Elon Musk’s SpaceX wants to operate in Poland, benefit from the Polish market, and earn from Polish customers, it must treat them fairly and on equal terms,” he added. “That is why I have appealed to SpaceX for the urgent restoration of equal terms for the company’s Polish customers.” Nie zgadzam się, żeby globalna firma technologiczna traktowała Polki i Polaków gorzej niż innych Europejczyków. Jeżeli @SpaceX @Elon Musk chce działać w Polsce, korzystać z polskiego rynku i zarabiać na polskich klientach, musi ich traktować uczciwie i na równych zasadach. Od… — Krzysztof Gawkowski (@KGawkowski) August 12, 2026 Meanwhile, foreign minister Radosław Sikorski revived a dispute he had with Musk last year over the provision of Starlink terminals to Ukraine during its war with Russia. That dispute saw Musk tell Sikorski to “be quiet, small man”. “Hey, Elon Musk, big man,” wrote Sikorski today on X, “stop discriminating [against] Polish users of Starlink or we might re-think paying you $50 million p.a. for your services.” The latter was a reference to the fact that Poland spends around $50 million a year to help provide Starlink services for Ukraine. World.title: Negative views of Polish-Ukrainian relations reach highest level on record in Poland
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. The proportion of Poles who hold a negative view of Polish-Ukrainian relations has risen to 46%, the highest figure ever recorded by Polish state research agency CBOS. Only 12% think relations are good. By contrast, three years ago, in mid-2023, only 3% had a negative view and 64% a positive one. Meanwhile, CBOS also found that belief among Poles that reconciliation between the two neighbours, who share a difficult history, is possible is at its lowest level on record, 53%, down from 78% three years ago. The findings follow other polls showing worsening attitudes towards Ukraine and Ukrainians in Poland in recent years, and come amid an ongoing diplomatic crisis triggered by President Volodymyr Zelensky naming a military unit after a group that massacred Poles in World War Two. Przekonanie o możliwości pojednania między Polakami 🇵🇱 a Ukraińcami 🇺🇦 spadło do najniższego poziomu w historii naszych pomiarów. 📙 Więcej w komunikacie #CBOS "Stosunki polsko-ukraińskie" ⤵️ https://t.co/kw2o4upY3Q#Ukraina #Ukraińcy pic.twitter.com/LItCFC3f2m — CBOS (@CBOS_Info) August 11, 2026 Relations between Poland and Ukraine improved significantly in the wake of Russia’s full-scale invasion in February 2022, as Poland welcomed millions of Ukrainian refugees and provided Kyiv with extensive military, humanitarian and diplomatic support. However, since 2023, those relations have been hit by a series of controversies over Ukrainian agricultural exports, border blockades by Polish farmers and truckers, and, above all, over the two nations’ difficult World War Two history. Among Poles who now hold a negative view of relations, CBOS also asked them who was responsible for the situation. A large majority, 65%, primarily blamed Ukraine, while only 4% said it was Poland’s fault and 28% placed responsibility on both sides. In its regular surveys since 1997, the agency has also asked Poles if they believe that reconciliation between Poles and Ukrainians is possible or not. In the early 2000s, that figure rose to a record level of 81%, and in 2023 it still stood at 78%. Now, however, it has dropped to an all-time low of 53%. There have long been tensions between Poland and Ukraine over their difficult, intertwined histories, in particular during the first half of the 20th century. In World War Two, Ukrainian nationalists killed around 100,000 Polish civilians, mostly women and children, in an ethnic-cleansing operation known as the Volhynia massacres. Poland has officially recognised that episode as a genocide. However, Ukraine rejects that label and also points to the persecution of Ukrainians who lived in the interwar Polish state, as well as to massacres of Ukrainians by Polish groups during World War Two. Long-simmering tensions between Poland and Ukraine over WWII massacres have finally boiled over, prompting a diplomatic crisis.@danieltilles1 looks at how we got here and what it may mean for the two countries and Europe more broadly https://t.co/a8tiYJJHRr — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 22, 2026 Those tensions recently boiled over after Zelensky, in May this year, approved a request to rename a military unit after the “heroes of the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA)”, the group that led the Volhynia massacres but is remembered positively in Ukraine for its role in fighting Moscow-imposed Soviet rule. Zelensky’s decision prompted his Polish counterpart, Karol Nawrocki, to strip the Ukrainian president of Poland’s highest honour. While tensions have since calmed somewhat, the dispute remains unresolved. However, even before that diplomatic crisis broke out, polling showed increasingly negative attitudes in Poland towards both Ukraine and Ukrainians, who are by far the country’s largest immigrant group. In its annual survey of attitudes towards various national and ethnic groups, published in February, CBOS found that the proportion of Poles who said they disliked Ukrainians had increased by five percentage points year-on-year, to 43%. Only 29% said they liked Ukrainians. In January, CBOS reported that opposition to accepting Ukrainian refugees in Poland had risen to its highest ever level. In December 2024, a poll in Ukraine found that positive sentiment towards Poles had fallen by half in the space of two years. The proportion of Poles opposed to accepting Ukrainian refugees has reached its highest ever level of 46%, up from 3% in the wake of Russia's full-scale invasion. Other recent surveys have also indicated declining sympathy towards Ukrainians among Poles https://t.co/DLPGY2ToZG — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 7, 2026 Meanwhile, the number of reported hate crimes against Ukrainians in Poland rose by 30% in the first half of 2026, including a number of high-profile incidents. Poland’s government has blamed increasing anti-Ukrainian rhetoric from the right-wing and far-right opposition. Last month, Ukraine’s foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha, called on “Polish politicians to stop inciting hatred against Ukrainians”. CBOS’s new study shows that attitudes towards relations with Ukraine differ significantly depending on political affiliation. Whereas 35% of supporters of the centrist Civic Coalition (KO), Poland’s main ruling party, hold a negative view of relations, that rises to 52% among voters of the national-conservative opposition Law and Justice (PiS) party and 81% for the far-right Confederation (Konfederacja). Among those with a negative view, 49% of KO voters blamed Poland and Ukraine equally for the situation while 10% blamed mainly Poland. By contrast, 86% of Confederation supporters and 82% of PiS supporters placed responsibility on the Ukrainian side. Demonstrations took place in 25 Polish cities on Sunday against the “growing wave of hate and violence” against Ukrainians, who are Poland’s largest immigrant group. Reported hate crimes against Ukrainians in Poland are up 30% this year https://t.co/gGAEc6QZWT — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 10, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Poland unveils first warship under major naval modernisation programme
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland has unveiled its first frigate to enter service in decades at a ceremony in the Baltic Sea port of Gdynia, where the ship was constructed. The development marks a major milestone in a 15 billion zloty (€3.5 billion) programme to modernise the ageing Polish navy and strengthen NATO’s maritime defences. “Poland is becoming a maritime power in the Baltic Sea,” declared Prime Minister Donald Tusk at a ceremony to name the new ship, which he attended alongside opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki in a rare show of unity. Na terenie PGZ Stoczni Wojennej w Gdyni prezydent RP Karol Nawrocki, @PremierRP @donaldtusk oraz wiceministrowie @MON_GOV_PL @magdasobkowiak i @pawelbejda uczestniczą w uroczystości chrztu pierwszej jednostki programu „Miecznik”, fregaty wielozadaniowej – przyszłego ORP Wicher. pic.twitter.com/X2ftjoKTLZ — Ministerstwo Obrony Narodowej 🇵🇱 (@MON_GOV_PL) August 12, 2026 The ORP Wicher, a medium-sized warship designed for escort, air defence and other fleet protection duties, is the first of three multi-role frigates based on Britain’s Arrowhead 140 design being built under Poland’s Miecznik programme, the largest modernisation project in the history of the Polish Navy. It is due to be launched on Thursday in a complex manoeuvre involving its transfer and controlled launch from a semi-submersible barge. Shipyard officials have described the operation as one of the most demanding engineering projects undertaken by Poland’s shipbuilding industry. The three frigates are intended to form the core of Poland’s surface fleet and will replace Poland’s two current Oliver Hazard Perry-class frigates, which were constructed in the 1970s and transferred from the US Navy in the years 2000 and 2002. Ahead of Wicher’s launch, leading Polish officials attended the naming ceremony in Gdynia, including Tusk and Nawrocki, who are normally bitter rivals but have sought to present a more united front when it comes to national defence. “There can be no arguments or disputes when it comes to our country’s security,” said Tusk, who declared that Poland was seeking to play a role in “determining not only its own future, but also the entire region and Europe”. Nawrocki, meanwhile, said that the modernisation of the Polish navy “sends a clear message that we will develop our armed forces in every theatre – on water, on land, and in the air”. Both leaders also hailed the fact that the new frigates are being built in Poland itself, helping bolster the Polish shipbuilding industry. Prezydent RP @NawrockiKn w #Gdynia: Życzę, abyście zawsze szczęśliwie wracali do portu, któremu na imię Polska. pic.twitter.com/hHia2sCZfn — Kancelaria Prezydenta RP (@prezydentpl) August 12, 2026 The contract for the three frigates was signed in 2021 between Poland’s state Armament Agency (AU) and a consortium led by state-owned defence group PGZ, with British defence firm Babcock and other foreign partners also involved. The project was initially valued at about 8 billion zloty but had risen to around 15 billion zloty by the end of 2023 following amendments. Construction of the second frigate in Gdynia’s military shipyard began in May 2025, while work on the third began in April this year. The programme is scheduled to be completed by the end of 2031. Swedish defence giant Saab has signed a strategic collaboration agreement with Polish state defence group PGZ. The firms will cooperate on naval production, servicing and technology, including establishing an underwater technology centre in Poland https://t.co/dykKjMIAzX — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 15, 2026 The ships are more than 140 metres long and are based on Britain’s Arrowhead 140 design, developed by Babcock and adapted to Polish military requirements. The frigates will be equipped with British CAMM and CAMM-ER surface-to-air missiles, naval guns and anti-ship missiles capable of striking targets at ranges of more than 200 km. Their missions will include protecting shipping lanes and critical energy infrastructure and taking part in NATO naval groups. NATO has launched a new military operation in the Baltic Sea, an idea promoted by Poland last year in response to sabotage targeting undersea cables.@donaldtusk said at today's summit that "all signs point to Russia" being responsible for the damage https://t.co/cBPdL1fKkK — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 14, 2025 Since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Poland has embarked on a major defence procurement spree. It now has the highest relative defence budget in NATO and is also the alliance’s largest arms importer. In recent years, Poland has also increasingly oriented itself towards the Baltic region, forming closer economic, energy and military ties with allies around the sea. Last year, Poland and Sweden signed a strategic partnership on defence and economic ties. They subsequently held their first ever bilateral military exercises in the Baltic. As part of its naval modernisation programme, Poland has selected Sweden’s Saab as the supplier for three advanced A26 stealth submarines in a deal worth around €4.5 billion. Poland has signed a €4.5 billion deal to buy three A26 submarines from Sweden.
